Abstract

We describe uo-harness, an AI agent harness that plays the Ultima Online free shard Outlands through a localhost proxy between the stock game client and the server. Deterministic Python runners do the reflex work: walking, chopping trees, fleeing, storing. They act on a world model built from server packets and a single SQLite memory that every part of the system shares. A Bayesian planner (Thompson sampling over lumber spots, with a renewal-reward trip size under competing death, sent-home and theft hazards) decides where to go and how long to stay. An LLM overseer, the Seer, sits outside the inner loop on a database message bus. It wakes at junctures, talks to the owner through a web visualizer and Telegram, and consults a knowledge base distilled from the community Discord through hybrid semantic search. The whole system was built in ten days by one person directing AI coding agents, mainly Claude Opus, with Kimi and Sonnet for some jobs: 568 human prompts became 389 commits and about 56k lines of Python. Over 88 logged-in hours the harness chopped 32,676 logs, stored 23,003 boards from 86 recorded lumber trips, raised a character's Lumberjacking from 50.1 to 95.6, answered 67 of 67 harvest CAPTCHAs, and died 12 times, three of them to the same player-killer. We report what worked, what we got wrong first, and what it was like to let the agents work out most of the implementation decisions.

1Introduction

On a Sunday evening in late September 2026 the owner of this repository typed a one-paragraph prompt into an AI coding agent: build an agent harness that plays Ultima Online Outlands, research how, and present a plan. Ten days and 389 commits later, a character named Character Omega was recalling out of a guild house rune library to a forest a few hundred tiles away, chopping trees as fast as the server allows, running from air dragons, fleeing player-killers, carrying boards home to a rented room, and reporting all of it to an LLM overseer that styles itself after Hawkwind the Seer. Nobody modified the game client.

Goal: create an AI agent harness that plays Ultima Online Outlands. […] Research how best to accomplish this and present a high level plan.

— the founding prompt, 2026-09-27 19:18 (laptop session log)

This paper is the long-form record of how that happened: what we built, the techniques we borrowed and invented, the many things we got wrong first, and what the numbers say so far. "We" means the owner and the fleet of coding agents he directed; the split of credit is itself one of the subjects (§11).

1.1Why this is harder than it sounds

Ultima Online (1997) is one of the first graphical MMOs: an isometric tile world (Outlands' main map is 10,752 × 6,144 tiles; stock UO's is 7,168 × 4,096), skills that rise with use, and full-loot player-versus-player. Outlands is a popular free shard (a privately run server) with its own client fork. §2 has the details.

Game bots are old news, and Ultima Online has had macro assistants since the last century. What made this project interesting is the combination of constraints we accepted (some on day one, some along the way):

  • The client is a fortress. The Outlands build of ClassicUO is compiled ahead of time to native code (NativeAOT). There is no .NET intermediate language to decompile, no runtime to hook, and no sanctioned plugin surface. We decided early never to inject into it, never to patch it, never to send synthetic keyboard or mouse input to its window, and never to write a byte into its install directory.
  • The server must see a normal client. Everything the harness does has to arrive at the server as packets the stock client could have sent, in the order and shape it sends them, interleaved with the human's own traffic on the same connection.
  • The agent must never reveal itself. No injected speech that mentions harnesses, testing or AI; a standing rule since day two AGENTS.md Constraint 4.
  • The world is hostile. Outlands has full-loot PvP, thieves who pick pockets, monsters that wander into lumber groves, harvesting CAPTCHAs, and staff who watch for unattended play.
  • The code has to explain itself. Every engineering finding is written down and pushed before a session ends (Rule 0), so that a fresh agent with no memory of the conversation can carry on. That rule is why this paper could be written at all.

1.2The system at a glance

The architecture we settled on is a man-in-the-middle of the most boring kind: a localhost TCP proxy (Figure 1). A WinDivert NAT quietly redirects the stock client's game connection to the proxy, which decrypts both directions and decompresses the server's, keeps a packet-built world model, and lets deterministic Python "runners" inject their own actions into the client's stream. A SQLite memory store records every event and doubles as a message bus. An LLM overseer, the Seer, sits outside the inner loop: it is woken at important junctures, reads the store through a small CLI, and decides what job to run next, while the runners do the reflexes.

Two design choices carry most of the weight. First, the proxy never originates a server-visible packet of its own: it forwards the client's traffic, it writes the agent's packets in the stock client's exact shapes, and the only thing it ever withholds is a duplicate reply to a target cursor the agent already answered. The fiction that keeps the client's screen honest (for example, a fake "you can't walk there" re-anchor after an agent step) is fabricated toward the client only. Second, the LLM decides what to do next, and deterministic code does it. The LLM picks the job, starts and stops it, and handles the situations the runners report; chopping, walking, fleeing and storing are deterministic controllers with typed failures. An LLM making those moment-to-moment moves would be slow, expensive and, as one dungeon fight demonstrated, fatal (§8).

1.3What this paper contributes

Most of what follows is engineering narrative, but a few pieces are, we think, worth stealing:

  1. A memory the whole system shares. One SQLite store that every component writes into and the overseer reads from: 2.1 million events, walk and harvest memory, trips, junctures, chat, and a knowledge table with hybrid semantic search on the GPU that also holds facts vetted from the community Discord. Beside it sit a local triage model (Laya) and the raw Discord corpus in its own database (§5, §9).
  2. Two senders, one character. A proxy that lets a human and an agent drive the same avatar at once, on one shared walk sequence and fast-walk key ladder, with client-only fabrications that keep the client's view consistent (§3). Re-framing all 65 non-empty captured client streams offline with the final length table (515,303 packets) gives zero client-to-server framing desyncs, and live the proxy logged none after the 09-29 length-table fix (47 sessions, about 82 h); before that fix two targets were misframed without being flagged.
  3. A packet-built world model with real 3-D pathfinding from the client's own map files, houses included, and rune libraries read without ever casting a spell (§4).
  4. A loop learned from demonstration and hardened against the shard's hazards, with a CAPTCHA solver that went 57 for 57 (§6.7), then made self-optimizing: Thompson sampling over lumber spots, competing death, sent-home and theft hazards, and a renewal-reward trip size (§6, §7).
  5. Survival engineering measured against an actual player-killer: recall-on-sight in about two seconds, a thief guard, keep-away from monsters (§8).
  6. An LLM overseer on a database bus: junctures, a CLI, a phone bridge and a vetted knowledge base distilled from the community Discord (§9, §5.6).
  7. A field report on building it with AI agents: 568 human prompts, 54 top-level sessions and 92 subagents, in which the owner set the goals and made the product and risk calls, and the agents worked out most implementation designs within them inferred (the record holds 32 "user decision" or "(user, …)" attribution markers in docs/NOTES.md and 19 commit messages with such a marker at ee59524, but no tally of agent-originated decisions), including a loop where the Seer's reports from the field became runner fixes within the hour (§11).

1.4How to read this

§2 is a crash course in Ultima Online for people who missed 1997. §3 through §9 walk up the stack from the network connection to the overseer; each chapter can be read alone. §10 collects the numbers, §11 is about the human–agent collaboration, and §12 covers lessons, limitations and the uncomfortable parts. The appendices hold a timeline, a repository map, a protocol reference, the planner's Bayesian model with its notation (Appendix D), a glossary (Appendix E) and the references (Appendix F).

2Background: Ultima Online for the rest of us

Just enough Ultima Online to follow the rest of the paper: the game, the shard, the client, the protocol, and the cast of characters.

2.1The game

Ultima Online (Origin Systems, 1997) is one of the first graphical MMOs and still one of the strangest. The world is a grid of tiles (on Outlands the main map, facet 0, is 10,752 × 6,144 of them; the stock Britannia map is 7,168 × 4,096) seen from an isometric camera, with height levels, buildings, caves and dungeons stacked in the z axis. There are no classes. A character's skills (Lumberjacking, Magery, Tracking and some fifty others) start low and rise by being used, so a character that chops trees for hours becomes a better lumberjack, slowly. Death is a big deal: you become a ghost, and anything not "blessed" or "newbied" stays on your corpse for whoever gets there first. Other players can attack you almost anywhere outside guarded towns. A player who kills other players a lot is flagged as a murderer and shown with a red name; the community calls them PKs (player-killers). A player who steals or attacks innocents turns grey for a while. Everyone else is blue.

Recall is the teleport spell that moves you to a marked rune. A runebook holds 16 marked locations; a rune tome holds more. A rune library is a shelf of public tomes in someone's house. See Appendix E for the rest of the jargon.

Travel is mostly by foot, by horse, through moongates, or by casting Recall on a marked rune. Interaction is through gumps (the generic UO dialog box), target cursors ("what do you want to use this on?"), context menus, and the journal, where the server prints what happens to you, mostly as numbered localized messages (clilocs).

2.2Outlands, ClassicUO and Razor

The official servers still run, but much of the remaining population plays on free shards: independently run servers with their own rules and content. UO Outlands is one of the largest and most heavily customized. It ships its own launcher (with an OutlandsID account system and e-mail device verification) and its own build of ClassicUO [7], the open-source C# reimplementation of the UO client. Unlike upstream ClassicUO, the Outlands build is compiled ahead of time to native code with .NET NativeAOT, so there is no plugin surface to build on, which is why the harness lives on the network instead (§3). At the start of the project the client was version 1.0.2.544; the launcher patched it to 1.0.2.550 a day later.

Razor [19] is the classic UO "assistant": macros, hotkeys, a scripting language. Outlands compiles a fork of Razor CE into its client and treats it as the only sanctioned automation surface; it also restricts what Razor scripts may do (walking was removed from Razor on Outlands in 2023, for example). That fact turns out to shape the harness: anything a Razor script can do at Razor's speed is, in a sense, normal behaviour on this shard, and anything beyond that is not.

Outlands documents its anti-automation stance in its rules and wiki: no unsanctioned tools, no unattended harvesting, CAPTCHAs that interrupt resource gathering every few minutes (three failures block harvesting for six hours), and staff who check on suspicious gatherers in person. §6.7 covers how the harness deals with CAPTCHAs and §6.8 with the chance of a staff member walking up.

2.3The protocol in one page

The client talks to the game server over a single long-lived TCP connection on port 2593. The protocol is old, binary and refreshingly simple. Every message is a packet that starts with a one-byte id. Most ids have a fixed length known to both sides; variable-length packets carry a two-byte length right after the id. The server compresses everything it sends with a static Huffman code that dates from 1997. Outlands wraps both directions in an additional per-session XOR layer (more in §3), widens about two dozen standard packets with extra fields, and adds a few of its own.

The walk handshake is the one piece of protocol everyone in this paper ends up knowing by heart. Each 0x02 carries a direction, a sequence number (0 after a reset, then 1–255, wrapping to 1) and a "fast-walk key" that the server handed out earlier.

A handful of packets do most of the work. Moving is a request (0x02) that the server either confirms (0x22) or denies (0x21, which also snaps you back to where the server thinks you are). Using an object is a double-click (0x06); many actions then open a target cursor (0x6C) that the client answers with whatever you clicked on. Dialogs arrive as gump packets (0xB0/0xDD) and are answered with a button press (0xB1). The server describes the world with mobile and item packets (0x20, 0x78, 0xF3 and friends) and narrates events with cliloc messages (0xC1/0xCC). A full list of what the harness reads and writes is in Appendix C.

2.4Venues and the cast of characters

New Outlands characters start on Shelter Island with Young status: no hostile player actions are possible there, the bank and vendors serve only Young characters, skills cap at 80 and the harvest chance is halved. Leaving the island renounces Young status permanently, after a two-click confirmation that the harness was never allowed to press. There is also a Test Shard with a player editor for setting skills and spawning items, which we used for the first week of experiments. Five characters appear in the data (Table 1).

The places that recur are Shelter Island (start zone, inn and bank), Horseshoe Bay (the first mainland lumber spot), the Terran wilds and Nusero (where Bastet hunted), Wintertop (a death), and dozens of forest clearings near the community's "Witcher" rune set that the planner explores (§7).

3The wire

Everything the harness knows and everything it does passes through one asyncio process on localhost. This chapter shows how the stock client was put on that wire, how the stream is decoded (including the day we spent decoding it wrong), and how agent packets are spliced in so the server sees one ordinary client while the client is quietly kept in step.

3.1Why a proxy

The first commit (e937fba, 2026-09-27 21:47) was an anti-cheat research report, and it set one rule before any code existed: the Outlands client stays 100% stock. The Outlands build of ClassicUO is compiled to native code (NativeAOT), so that rule ruled out most of the obvious designs (Table 2).

A proxy sees what the client sees, and an injected packet is, on the wire, the same thing as a key press. The price is speaking the Outlands protocol perfectly in both directions. This chapter is about how the harness does that.

3.2Getting in the middle

The plan assumed upstream ClassicUO's -ip/-port arguments. On 2026-09-28 the Outlands fork turned out to ignore them, and settings.json too. The game server's address arrives as a literal IP in the HTTPS login response, and play.uooutlands.com "does not exist in DNS at all" docs/INTERCEPTION.md, so there is no name to hijack either.

WinDivert [27] is a signed Windows driver that lets a user-mode program intercept and rewrite IP packets. divert_nat.py is 88 lines of pydivert on top of it and has to run elevated.

So the redirect moved below the client, into the kernel. harness/divert_nat.py catches outbound TCP to port 2593, rewrites both addresses to 127.0.0.1, and remembers which server IP S each client source port P was dialling; a return rule undoes it. Rewriting only the destination failed silently, because Windows drops loopback-destination packets with a non-loopback source as martians. The proxy dials out from ports 25940–25960, which the filter excludes, so its own traffic doesn't loop.

The first NAT matched one server IP, 74.91.115.123. On 2026-09-30 at 22:14 the client went to 35.71.142.123 instead, around the proxy "with no error shown", and twelve minutes later to 52.223.17.219. By 22:29 the NAT diverted any IP on :2593 (d0c7eb9), and the proxy asks its lookup service on :25943 which IP the client meant, dials that, and drops connections the NAT doesn't know. Across the 69 session logs the upstream split 35 / 19 / 15 between the three addresses. No payload byte changes; the server sees the player's IP with a different source port, like any home router.

Ports: 2593 game listen; 25940–25960 upstream source ports; 25941 control (agent packets in); 25942 state (JSON out); 25943 NAT lookup. Full reference in Appendix C.

Inside, harness/proxy.py is one asyncio process: 218 lines at Phase 1 (0663786), 1,087 now. A SessionTap per connection decodes both directions packet by packet, feeds the world model (§4), and logs every packet plus the raw wire, flushed on every call "so a killed proxy loses nothing". World-model exceptions are caught: "relay must survive any model bug".

3.3Two ciphers, one of them a compressor

The two directions are obfuscated differently. Client to server (C2S): a 5-byte cleartext preamble, then every byte XORed with one per-session key, ci=pi⊕︎S (we had first modelled a per-position keystream; "one byte explains everything"). Server to client (S2C): a 13-byte cleartext prelude carrying both keys, then every byte XORed with K and run through UO's standard static Huffman code.

prelude  ff 00 0d 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 0c K S    (K = S2C key, S = C2S key)
C2S      ef 00 00 00 0c | packets ^ S
S2C      prelude | per packet: Huffman(packet) FLUSH pad-to-byte, all ^ K

The S2C property everything later depends on: each server packet is compressed on its own and ends in the flush symbol, padded to a byte boundary, so one flush segment is exactly one packet. The proxy can forward a packet's original wire bytes, drop it, or substitute encode_packet(new) without touching the rest of the stream. Re-measured on session 20261001_191355, harness/uo/s2c.py decodes 1,298,764 raw bytes into 83,929 packets with no leftover bytes, and re-encoding reproduces the wire with 0 mismatches (compression ratio 0.683).

3.4The phantom dialect

For the first day we didn't know that, and the decode we had looked fine. The Phase 1 proxy (0663786, 2026-09-28 12:09) started Huffman at byte 19 and applied no XOR. A static Huffman tree decodes any bit string, and garbage throws up a flush symbol every so often, so out came a steady supply of "packets"; a length table extended "by desync search" framed them "cleanly" for long runs. By evening there was a story: Outlands spoke a custom S2C dialect, with a "world-state stream" of ids 0x00/0x40/0x3F/0x52, one-off 13,155-byte and 30,627-byte "dumps" plus a recurring family of ~100-byte records, a MessagePack hypothesis, and a commit titled "World-state stream resolved (negative result)" (9265c57, 18:22). Movement analysis then explained the missing fastwalk-key packets as "swallowed by the desynced regions".

One wrong assumption (no XOR, Huffman from byte 19) produced a self-consistent-looking but false picture that survived for a day.

— docs/PROTOCOL.md, lessons

The correction came from the client. The decompiled NetClient.ProcessRecv XORs every received byte with a key at NetClient+0x71 (prelude byte 11) before DecompressBuffer; upstream ClassicUO has no such step. Commit 5eb2138 (2026-09-29 15:04) fixed the decoder. Ten minutes later 8cc2724, "garbage-decode artifacts removed", deleted the wire-derived table entries (0x00=106, 0x6F=76, 0x9E=65, 0xDC=15) and the old decoder, fixed nine world-model parser layouts against real packets, and reduced docs/WORLDSTATE.md to a supersession notice: "All of that was decode garbage." On the capture where the old proxy had framed 103 S2C packets with 4 desyncs, the test fixture now asserts 2,835.

Lesson

A decode that frames is not a decode that is right. The rule we adopted: "Accept a decode only if it reproduces known plaintext and frames every capture end-to-end under the client's own length table without per-id guesses." The cheap check that would have caught it on day one was to look for the player's serial or name in the S2C stream. Once the stream is decoded correctly, those appear everywhere.

3.5A length table from the binary

UO packets are fixed-length by id or carry a big-endian u16 length at bytes 1–2, so framing needs a length table. We took it from the client's own packet table: 145 base entries, with protocol-version tiers on top. Twenty-two standard fixed-length ids carry Outlands values: against upstream, 19 of them are 1–16 bytes wider (0x6C target is 27 bytes, 0x08 drop 22), 0xEF is narrower (21 → 5), and 0x0B and 0xB9 keep their length.

The client pads what it sends to the same table, so C2S framing uses it too: C2S_OVERRIDES holds the 27 ids where Outlands differs from upstream. Until 2026-09-29 17:21 (f73f64e) the only override was 0x91, and a real 27-byte target framed as 19 bytes; "the rest of the captured target became an 0x00 'packet' of 106 bytes that swallowed the following client traffic". Re-framed offline with the current table, all 65 non-empty captured client streams (515,303 packets, 2026-09-28 → 2026-10-06 12:00 CDT) frame end to end with 0 desyncs. Live, the proxy has logged no desync since f73f64e (47 sessions, ≈82 h); before that fix, two 09-28 targets were misframed without being flagged, because the live detector only sees implausible lengths. When it does fire, the proxy logs it and forwards a byte anyway, so the relay never stalls.

3.6Injection discipline

An agent action enters as a plaintext packet on the control port: a u16be length prefix, the packet, and an OK or ERR <reason> reply. InjectionHub.inject applies the same order every time:

  1. Gate. AgentGate.block_reason() checks kill, pause, mandatory break and the 8 h/day budget (2ffb29a). Client traffic is never gated.
  2. Walk gate. For 0x02 walks, MoveAuthority.agent_walk_block checks pacing and in-flight steps (next subsection).
  3. Upstream write. The packet goes through exactly the client's path (same rewrite, log and XOR) and is spliced in between whole client packets, never inside one.
  4. Client-only fix-up. Only after the server write: a gump reply is followed by a fabricated gump close toward the client, and a target reply by a fabricated cursor cancel.

The packets come from harness/actions.py (527 lines), where "every builder returns the exact plaintext bytes a stock Outlands ClassicUO client would emit", with layouts from the decompiled NetClientExt.Send_* methods, checked against captures. The proxy never injects the ~1/s keepalive: it carries no timestamp, and its timing is left entirely to the client.

Decision, 2026-09-30

"Byte-correct packets weren't enough: the audit found sequences the client can't produce (a context menu without its click, replies with missing entries, a cursor answered twice, steps into walls…)." The rule since then: agent traffic reproduces what the stock client sends for the same UI gesture, including the packets that accompany it, and an action the client couldn't perform right now is refused rather than sent (37a2b00).

3.7One walk ladder for two walkers

A walk is 7 bytes: 02 <dir|0x80 run> <seq> <key u32>. The server answers with 0x22 ConfirmWalk or 0x21 DenyWalk.

Movement caused the most trouble. The client and the agent both send 0x02 walks on one TCP stream. The server accepts a walk only if its sequence number is the next one expected and, for the first walk after the server arms a token, its fastwalk key matches that token, a field stock RunUO ignores but which "on Outlands it is alive". The sequence wraps 0xFF → 1, resets to 0 on a seed (login, honored resync, teleport) or a deny, and rewinds after a silent rejection. The token is whatever the server's latest 0xBF sub 1 seed or sub 2 push armed: login usually ends on 8 (a 5, 6, 7, 8 burst) and most re-arms carry 1, but the server also sends 2–13, so the proxy copies the value from the seed rather than assuming the constants of the 09-29 model (9e0f3bf). Two independent senders on that ladder desync each other, and they did, in several ways (Table 3).

Two stages rested on beliefs that the corrected decode disproved. We had read the frozen client as a server-side "behavioral gate on walk trains"; with the server's packets visible, session 142237 showed all 12 agent walks confirmed while the client drew nothing. "The lockout was 100% client-side": the client freezes when it gets a 0x22 for a step it never took. And fix B needed the S2C stream editable packet by packet, which the phantom had made look impossible. Fix B and the decode correction landed in the same commit.

The current design lives in MoveAuthority. Every walk from either sender gets pkt[2] = next_seq on one ladder; the first walk after a seed carries the armed token, and the client's leftover copy is zeroed once "so the server never sees a spent token". The server's confirm for an agent step is hidden from the client and replaced by a fabricated 0x21 DenyWalk at the tracked server-true position. The client's handler resets its walker and calls SetInWorldTile: a teleport-in-place it accepts without complaint. (A fabricated self 0x20 would have been simpler, but the V10 handler ignores position for the player.) Client confirms are rewritten back to the client's own sequence. A walk unconfirmed after 3 s counts as rejected and the ladder rewinds; three rejections in a row stall agent walking; at most 5 steps are in flight, the stock client's limit.

Re-anchoring only after quiet (the 16:08 design) had a visible cost. During long agent walks the client's picture lagged a median of 10 tiles (max 53) behind the character, so it dropped mobiles it thought out of range and closed their status bars within 10 ms of the click: 93% of the time during agent walking, against 1–5% in human sessions, "a per-mobile signature a server log sees directly". A11 re-anchors on every hidden confirm and brought that to 0.3% (6 of 2,072). Its own side effect: each re-anchor re-fired the client's Auto Open Doors and Auto Open Corpses, so both were switched off and the Mover opens doors itself.

3.8Two views of one session

The server and the client thus see different sessions on purpose (Table 4).

Target cursors needed the most care. When the server raises a cursor (a spell, a hatchet) and the agent answers it, the client's cursor is still up, and a later click would send a second reply to a cursor the server already consumed: "a stock client can't reply to one cursor twice". The 09-30 audit found exactly that 4 times in one session. Cancelling only the client's copy is not enough, because the stock client answers a cancel with its own C2S cancel. So the proxy sends the client the server's exact cancel, marks the cursor id spent, and drops the client's reply to it (Figure 6). That is the only client packet the current proxy drops; a resync-suppression test on the morning of 09-29 once dropped a client resync.

It balances exactly. Across all 69 logs there are 8,267 fabricated cancels and 8,267 dropped client replies, a 1:1 match, mirrored in the memory store's event table. In the 20261001_191355 audit, all 479 agent target answers went to live server cursors and 0 client 0x6C replies were relayed.

3.9Traffic and timing

423,349C2S packets relayed from the client
94,295C2S packets injected by agents
2.62MS2C packets from the server
65,534client-only fabrications, never sent upstream
0C2S desyncs re-framing 515,303 captured client packets

Over the 69 session logs on this machine (2026-09-28 → 2026-10-06 12:00 CDT, 87.6 hours connected), the agent produced 18% of what the server received. Over two thirds of that (65,495) were walks; then come 0x06 double-clicks (9,055) and 0x6C targets (8,403). The client-only stream breaks down into 55,016 re-anchors, 8,267 cursor cancels and 2,251 gump closes. Figure 7 splits both by day. The right panel also shows the A11 change: on 09-30 the proxy hid 10,501 agent confirms but sent only 1,558 re-anchors. From 10-01 the two counts match to within 5 a day (the extra re-anchors are timer re-anchors after rejections and late confirms).

Walking is fast now. The median time from an agent walk to the server's confirm is 46–63 ms across three big sessions, about one network round trip (keepalive RTT medians 46–66 ms on the same sessions), i.e. the server confirms at once. The maxima of 3.2–3.5 s are server pauses (on 10-01, documented world saves). They exceed the 3 s confirm timeout, which was raised from the 1.5 s first tried after 2.0–2.3 s hitches, so such a walk is first counted as rejected and then recovered by the 5 s late-confirm window. Above the proxy's floors, the Mover adds the stock held-key cadence plus 3–15 ms of jitter, giving a median gap of 0.248 s on foot and 0.117 s mounted (6917539). A human running on foot has a median of about 0.200 s.

Lines of code at ee59524 (2026-10-06): proxy.py 1,087; actions.py 527; agent_link.py 930; agent_gate.py 237; uo/s2c.py 118; uo/packets.py 107; divert_nat.py 88.

The wire layer is small: about 2,000 lines across the proxy, NAT, codec, tables and action builders, out of about 36,000 in the harness (49,000 with its tests). proxy.py has not changed since 10-02. The rest of the system builds on it: the world model reads what the server saw (§4), the runners and the Seer act through port 25941 (§6, §9), and the cross-cutting results are in §10.

4World model and maps

The agent knows only what the stock client knows, rebuilt from packets, and it walks only where the client would let it walk, from map files we had to reverse-engineer first. Everything it experiences is handed on to the memory store (§5).

4.1A mirror of the client, not a better client

The world model (harness/world/) is a packet-driven copy of the client's state. It is not a game engine and not a cheat: its ground truth is the stock client's own handlers, decompiled, and the rule is that the harness never acts on anything the client has already forgotten. The field layouts came from the decompiled NativeAOT client plus upstream ClassicUO and Razor sources, and every field carries a confidence label: upstream, decomp or unknown. Layouts branch on a protocol version dword set during the handshake. Live Outlands reports 12, and many packets are longer than upstream (0xF3 world item 26→38 bytes, 0xC0 effect 36→52, 0x20 mobile update 19→28, and so on) docs/WORLDMODEL.md.

Declarative tables (layouts.py) feed one bounds-checked big-endian reader; procedural parsers cover list and flag packets. WorldRuntime dispatches 46 server-to-client and 17 client-to-server packet ids into a StateStore: self (position, vitals, gold, weight, facet, skills), mobiles, items as a container tree, open gumps (UO's server-defined dialog windows), the target cursor, buffs and names: "Last-write-wins entity snapshots plus the lazy name map." Client traffic counts as input too: a walk request stays pending until the server's 0x22 confirm, and the self position moves only on confirms, which matched the proxy's own position at all 23,652 settled points of a replay 1520d7e.

Each change also comes out as an event: the world model emits item_seen, delete, speech_heard, death, …, and the proxy's MoveAuthority adds its own step and blocked events. The proxy keeps the newest 5,000 in a ring for state-port readers and hands every one to the memory store, which keeps them all and derives walk evidence from the steps and denies (§5.3). The overseer's "journal" is just a filter over that stream (ctl journal).

The 18-tile view range was a surprise: Outlands sends c8 12, against ClassicUO's default of 24.

Forgetting was the subtle part. On 2026-10-01 the overseer cast Lightning at mongbats that the model still held and the client had long dropped, and the server answered "That is too far away." Since then the model prunes exactly as the decompiled World.ProcessDeletes does: on the roughly once-a-second 0xFF sub 5 tick and on every self move, drop whatever lies beyond the view range set by S2C 0xC8. All 395 range prunes in one session landed within −0.68 to +0.06 s of the client's own close-status packet for the same serial docs/WORLDMODEL.md "Pruning".

A cautionary footnote: on 2026-09-28 we spent an evening documenting an Outlands "world-state stream" of 106-byte records that turned out, the next afternoon, to be decode garbage from a skipped XOR (§3). With the corrected decode, all 18 captures (53,277 packets) parse with zero failures.

4.2Upstairs, and the map in 34 minutes

Until 2026-09-29 the harness walked by a 2-D "walk memory": tiles and edges it had seen the server confirm. The first live lumber attempt ended that era. At 21:23 the character Character Alpha left its rental room and came out upstairs in the Shelter Island inn, at (1938, 2584, z 20). The walk memory knew only the ground floor at those x, y, so "A* kept routing through upstairs walls": 21 blocked moves, then ABORTED: too many blocked moves. Worse, the 40 upstairs blocks it had learned would have poisoned ground-floor routes, so that change was reverted docs/LUMBER_LOOP.md §13.

the harness needs the full x/y/z Outlands map, like the client has, for its own pathfinding and to find trees to harvest.

— user directive, recorded in docs/LUMBER_LOOP.md, 2026-09-29

Outlands ships none of the standard map*.mul, statics*.mul or tiledata.mul files; the client reads proprietary .uoo containers through its own UOO.* classes. An agent read those loaders in Ghidra [12] and committed a working mmap reader at 21:49, 26 minutes after the abort, with 42 checks against capture evidence (tree targets, inn floors at z 0 and 20, stairs, a sunken area at −20). The 3-D pathfinder followed at 21:57 f92f680 216f26c. Table 5 lists the differences from the classic formats.

Facet 0, the main world, holds 10,773,929 statics. Two findings shaped the rest of the code. Facet 3 is a blank placeholder of impassable land, yet the rental rooms live there, so the old walk memory survives as the planner for rooms. And doors are not statics at all but dynamic items sent by the server docs/MAP.md.

4.3Walking like the client

harness/pathfind.py ports ClassicUO's Pathfinder.cs (CreateItemList, CalculateMinMaxZ, CalculateNewZ, CanWalk), with z widened to int as in the Outlands build. The land surface is "stretched" between its four corner heights (top = own tile, right, left, bottom), and the walkable average takes the flatter diagonal:

zavg={⌊(ztop+zbottom)/2⌋|ztop−zbottom|≤|zleft−zright|⌊(zleft+zright)/2⌋otherwise
(1)

A capture confirmed it: the server put us at z 10 on a tile whose raw land z is 11 (corners 11/10/10/10). new_z then chooses, among the land, surfaces and bridges on the target tile, the one whose height is closest to the current z and leaves 16 units of clearance (one body) under the next blocker. The proof set: all 1,249 server-confirmed moves in the walk memory are walkable, all 20 non-door denies upstairs are walls, and a route from upstairs to the innkeeper exists. The same Walkers object also gives the proxy a z for every confirmed step, because 0x22 confirms carry none; before that, the proxy's z was wrong at 12 of 57 live anchors d602ea8.

Planning is plain heap A* over (x, y, z) with 8 neighbours. A diagonal costs the same as a straight step, as on the server. Costs are shaped rather than forbidden:

MOBILE_COST_X  = 4.0    # tile occupied by a mobile (they move)
DANGER_COST_X  = 30.0   # inside a creature's danger zone
SHOVE_RETRY_S  = 15.0   # a denied shove makes the tile a wall this long
MOBILE_WAIT_S  = 90.0   # a route cut only by mobiles is waited out
max_expand     = 30000  # A* node budget (3-D)

Per-plan humanizer noise scales these, and nav.straighten irons out zig-zags (agent paths had 37% heading changes against 21% for a human). Server denies become blocked (x, y, dir) moves for the session. Each step is re-checked with CanWalk against items that arrived after planning, because the stock client never sends a step it would refuse. Doors are opened ahead with the stock request; teleporters are learned by stepping (a landing that isn't the next tile) into the teleporters table. The map knows terrain but not spawns; the blind 250-tile goto through a harpy nest belongs to §8.

4.4Houses are multis

"Player houses block walking, and the map files don't show them." A house arrives as an 0xF3 item whose graphic indexes multi.mul, not art, and until 2026-10-02 the harness ignored its pieces. At Corpse Creek, house 0x154 drew 12 server denies on one trip, each step walkable on the bare map. Two bugs were stacked: the walk rules didn't expand multis, and the model pruned the house the instant it arrived at 22 tiles. The fix expands each 16-byte multi.mul record (graphic, dx, dy, dz, flags) into dynamic objects and keeps a house within view range plus its reach, as ClassicUO's HouseManager.IsHouseInRange does. Now the house is present at all 12 deny points, and routes enter houses by the front door docs/NOTES.md "Houses".

We rejected learning houses from denies: "It costs a deny burst per house, which no client produces, and a house can be placed or removed at any time." The last rule came from a death on 2026-10-05: an escape route ran through another player's door ("you can't walk into one uninvited", as the owner put it). Now every door on or beside a house we are not standing in is locked to the planner.

4.5Rune libraries: reaching the whole map

A rune marks a spot; casting Recall on it teleports you there. A rune tome or runebook holds many, and each recall spends mana or one of the book's charges.

Walking from banks reached little: 354 of 359 public treasure-map runes lie more than 110 tiles from every bank. The community "Witcher" rune set (runes 1–353 plus letter suffixes; a public table of 359 dig tiles) stands as 14 public tomes in the Cambria Rune Library. On 2026-10-04 Character Omega's guild library at the Guild house turned out to be much bigger: 36 locked-down tomes, 839 runes.

The trick that made libraries cheap was reading without recalling. In the rune-tome gump, row i's button 100+i recalls (and spends a charge), but 200+i opens the rune's detail page, which shows each rune's name and its tile "(x, y)". Button 5 pages on. ctl act read_tomes guild read all 36 tomes in 463 s, every tile, "with nothing cast and no charge spent." Runebooks show only sextant strings, which convert as

x=1323+lon⋅5120360,y=1624+lat⋅4096360
(2)

(east and south positive, wrapped), within one tile. Reading also showed that the guild's Witcher runes had been marked by someone else: 58 of 359 land away from the public table's tile (301 exact, 31 off by 1–5 tiles, 23 by 6–17, 3 by 18–40; rune 165 by 100). Hence the decision "a tome row's own tile is the only truth": one library table with rows per tome, and ambiguous names (20 repeat across Guild tomes) refused rather than guessed docs/PLAN.md "Rune libraries".

Home is data, not code. harness/data/homes.json maps each character to a landing (Character Omega's book's default rune, the "Guild Loot Chest" at (withheld)), its library, and a facet-3 rental room reached through the house steward. home.py counts anything within 60 tiles of the landing as home. Recall as the way out to a grove is in §7; recall as an escape is in §8.

5Memory

Everything the harness sees, does and concludes goes into one SQLite file. Deterministic code reads it to walk, chop and plan; the LLM reads a small, curated part of it through a ranked search. The store also serves as the message bus, the analytics warehouse, the training set and this paper's data source. This chapter covers how it is built, how each part is read, and what we can and cannot say about how well it works.

5.1Three memories and the line between them

Three different things in this project could be called memory (Table 7). The coding agents that built the harness remember through the git repository. The harness remembers through its runtime store, harness/data/harness.db. The Seer, the LLM that supervises the harness (§9), also has its context window, which lasts one session and gets compacted. This chapter is mostly about the second, but the boundaries between the three were deliberate design decisions.

The line between the first two came from a clarification by the owner. Rule 0 orders every coding session to "record and commit engineering knowledge". On 2026-09-29, when the store was built, the rule gained a second paragraph: it "does NOT cover the harness's own runtime memory … game state, what the agent learned while playing (walk/harvest memory, episodes, hazard stats), event logs and captures of its play" AGENTS.md:9; 7a3e26f. The repository keeps how the memory works (the code, docs/MEMORY.md) plus the captures that tests cite as evidence; the contents stay in a gitignored file. This keeps a 352 MB, fast-changing, partly personal data set out of a repository that agents read at the start of every session, and it means that a new checkout knows how to remember but has no memories. It is also why moving to a second computer needed its own tool (§5.8).

The line between the store and the context window is just as deliberate. A Seer's context does not outlive its session, and on 10-05 alone six numbered Seers played one after another (§9.6). Whatever one Seer should know about the previous one's work therefore has to be in the store. A new Seer starts with ctl status, the open junctures and ctl know brief, and the prompt makes it read and follow every pinned entry first docs/OVERSEER.md:376-379. Pinning was added on 10-04 at the owner's request because importance alone could not guarantee recall: 26 standing candidates were competing for the brief's 12 slots. The first pinned entry, #4079, is the procedure for using the guild's rune library 71e4207. How often the Seer's own context was compacted during shifts was not measured inferred: the compaction figures in §11.2 are for the coding sessions.

5.2One store, many roles

The store is SQLite in WAL mode with synchronous=NORMAL. It replaced three JSON/JSONL files (walk memory, harvest memory, lumber episodes) in one cut-over at 22:06 on 2026-09-29, the same evening as the map 7a3e26f.

Decision

SQLite, because it is durable (the WAL survives crashes), indexed, in the standard library, and lets the proxy, runners, viz, ctl, overseer and Telegram bridge all read concurrently while writers take turns (one writer at a time). Rejected: JSON files (walkmem.json "was 2D, facet-less and rewritten whole"), Postgres ("needs a service"), DuckDB ("analytics-first, not in the stdlib, single-writer file lock").

Schema growth without migrations. Every connection runs the whole schema as CREATE … IF NOT EXISTS and then writes schema_version harness/memory.py:166-174. A new table therefore appears the first time any process opens the store; there are no migration scripts. The schema went from v1 to v5 in 25 hours. After that, three more additions (guard_points, knowledge_vec, two time indexes) came without a version bump (Table 8). Columns were never altered. New fields went into JSON data columns, which is how a lumber trip row reached 47 keys without a schema change. One side effect: opening the store is itself a write. Anything that must not write (the backups, the Laya data builder and every query in this paper) uses a separate mode=ro connection.

The write path. The proxy is the heaviest writer and the one that must never stall, because it relays the game connection. Its MemoryWriter is built so that "the relay never waits on disk": record() puts the event envelope on an in-process queue and returns. A daemon thread with its own connection inserts each event, derives walk rows from it in the same transaction, and commits every 0.25 s or every 500 rows, whichever comes first harness/memory.py:512-586. Events are keyed on (session, seq) and inserted with INSERT OR IGNORE, so replaying a capture twice is harmless. A failed insert is counted in errors and skipped; nothing retries it. Runners write through the Memory class on their own connection and commit after every call, a harvest attempt or a trip row at a time. That is cheap at their rate, a few rows a minute.

Concurrency. WAL gives one writer at a time and any number of readers on the same host. Writers wait up to 30 s for the lock harness/memory.py:168. The store has six kinds of writer (proxy, runners, ctl, the Telegram bridge, the Discord pipeline, the capture ingester) and more readers. We found no record of a lock timeout in normal operation inferred: the docs mention "database is locked" only for the handoff's deliberate writer check, and the writer's error counter is not persisted. "Same host" turned out to be the real constraint, and it is why the store could not live on the NAS (§5.8).

Figure 11 groups the tables by the kind of memory they hold and shows who writes and who reads each group. The rest of the chapter follows those groups.

2,073,515events (world 1,752,109 / proxy 321,406)
22,739distinct facet-0 tiles stood on, from 32,735 walk rows
32,676logs from 4,125 successful chops, among 7,794 harvest rows
352 MBstore size at 2026-10-06 12:00 (backup-API copy, WAL included)

5.3Episodic memory: what happened

The event log. Every event the proxy's state port emits is stored as an envelope: session, sequence number, time, origin (world for the world model, proxy for the proxy's own movement and control logic), event name and a JSON payload. Here is a real row, a server-confirmed step north at 19:00:10 on 10-05, during a lumber trip to the spot witcher_23, and the walk row it created:

events     (session 66, seq 365982, t 1791244810.477, origin 'proxy', ev 'step',
            data {"ev": "step", "from": [1681, 660], "to": [1681, 659], "z": 1})
walk_moves (facet 0, x 1681, y 660, z 1, dir 0, ok 1)  n = 1, first_t = last_t = t

A second confirmation of the same move would only raise n and last_t harness/memory.py:178-205. The log holds 64 event kinds. It is not curated, and the volumes show it: the server's keepalives are the largest kind, 593,835 rows or 29% of the log; items coming into view (item_seen, 488,177), deletes (147,301) and animations (108,218) follow. By payload bytes, item_seen (24%) leads keepalives (20%). The payloads total 157 MB of JSON, about 76 bytes per event SELECT ev, count(*), sum(length(data)) FROM events WHERE t < 12:00 GROUP BY ev. We kept everything because nobody could say in advance which events would matter. That bet paid off several times (below).

Sessions and captures. The 69 sessions are 44 live proxy sessions and 25 older captures. python harness/memory.py ingest replays a capture through the proxy's own SessionTap and writes the rows a live session would have written; all 25 captures (70.6k events) took 7.7 s docs/MEMORY.md "Who writes what". Since live and replayed sessions go through the same code, the raw captures in logs/ are a second, lossless episodic memory, the bytes on the wire. Ten of them are committed as test fixtures, the only runtime data allowed in git under Rule 0 git ls-files logs; AGENTS.md:9.

Trip rows. episodes holds one JSON row per runner trip or hunt visit: 86 lumber rows and 36 hunt rows at the snapshot. The latest lumber row has 47 keys: spot, outcome and why, phase times (harvest, to_room, convert, store), walking and chopping seconds, steps and blocked moves, skill before and after, hatchet and its uses, travel legs, supplies, players seen, captchas, escapes, attempts, successes, logs, and the boards stored and stockpiled. On average a lumber row is 2.1 KB. The row is written in a finally block, so a trip that ends in an exception still leaves one harness/loop_lumber.py:3205, 3235-3247 at ee59524. That was not always so. Until 2026-10-02 only trips that reached the bank were recorded, and "leaving those out flattered exactly the spots where trips get cut short: of the 2026-10-02 Terran and Corpse Creek runs only the trips that banked were recorded" docs/LUMBER_LOOP.md:1219-1222. The size of that bias shows in the rows since: of the 68 lumber rows that carry an outcome, 45 are aborted, against 23 banked or stored. A process kill still writes nothing.

Everything else that happened. job_events (2,161 rows, 19 kinds) records facts that are not trips: Smart Harvest stands (1,142), kills (229) and loot (213) on hunts, speech holds and clears, flights, player-killer sightings, recalls, monster sightings and hits, thefts and deaths. junctures (377) and chat (3,021) are the overseer bus and the conversation; §5.7 covers them.

5.4Learned memory read by code, not by the model

Most of what the harness learns is never shown to the LLM. The runners and the planner read the store directly, with plain SQL and no prompt, so the system gets better from its own records without any model in the loop. Table 9 lists each piece of learned memory, where it is read and what it changes.

Walk evidence. walk_moves is keyed on (facet, x, y, z, direction, ok) with a hit count and first and last times. The projection the planner sees treats a move as blocked "only while its latest deny is newer than its latest confirm", because "doors and mobiles block only for a while" harness/memory.py:220-235. The human's walking teaches it as well as the agent's. Until the 3-D map arrived on the evening of 09-29, this was the only planner the harness had, and it failed the first time the character came out on an upper floor (§4.2). Today the map planner (§4.3) does not consult walk memory at all. The table still serves the rental rooms on facet 3, the viz's walk layer, and evidence: the map's walk rules were accepted because all 1,249 server-confirmed moves then in the table came out walkable.

Harvest memory and the planner. A tree tile that ran dry or proved unreachable is skipped until the regrowth window has passed. The window itself is learned: lumber_opt.regrowth pairs every depleted attempt with the next attempt on the same tree and fits P(regrown | gap) isotonically, giving 65 minutes at the snapshot (Figure 28). Each ctl lumber plan call reads every lumber trip row, every sighting, escape, theft and death, and the whole attempt table, then turns them into the posteriors of §7. At this scale, a few thousand rows, a full read costs less than keeping a cache in sync. Because every new row is evidence for the next plan, the quality of the records matters as much as the model. The survivorship fix above is one example; another is the rule that the Seer runs the planner's command "verbatim", because "hand-picked arguments spoil the data" (§9.1).

Recorded once, used later. Several consumers appeared after the data they read. guard_points came on 10-02, and python harness/guards.py backfill filled it by replaying the event log for the guard message, including events recorded before the table existed docs/MEMORY.md, guard_points row. Hatchet wear is read from speech_heard events that were stored for the journal. Laya's training set drew real player lines from the same events (§5.7). The meta table shows the opposite tendency: small learned facts (a character's books, landings that put us somewhere else, its pet) went in as JSON blobs under a key because no table fit them. That was quick to build but invisible to the schema.

5.5Semantic memory for the LLM: ctl know

The other tables record events. knowledge holds what the agent concluded: game knowledge and its dealings with players and the owner, kept across shifts docs/MEMORY.md "Knowledge". It is the only part of the store the LLM reads as memory, and it is built like a small agent-memory system: typed entries, provenance on each one, versioning instead of overwrites, and ranked hybrid retrieval. An example, the resurrection procedure as it stood at the snapshot:

#4095  procedure  "resurrection"   source user, confidence 0.9, importance 9, tags death healer
  "On death there's no gump and no Young transport; the ghost stays put and the corpse takes
   the gold. Walk the ghost to a healer (…): the Resurrection gump (Accept 1 / Decline 2) opens
   within 2 tiles; stand still, then ctl act gump <serial> 1; …"
  supersedes #4094 (10-05 11:07), which superseded #13 (09-30 10:38, from the Young demos)

Data model. Each entry has a kind (fact, procedure, episode, preference for a standing directive of the owner's, insight for a lesson drawn from episodes), a topic, the content, tags, the entities it is about, and optionally a location (facet, x, y). Provenance is a source_type plus a source_ref (capture tag, chat or juncture id, URL). Confidence starts at a prior for the source: user 0.95, observed 0.9, doc 0.8, wiki 0.7, community 0.6, inferred 0.5 harness/knowledge.py:54. The writer sets an importance from 1 to 10 ("how much it matters if forgotten"). status is active, superseded or retracted, and supersede links form a version chain. access_count and last_access_t record retrieval. A tag char:<name> scopes an entry to one character, and the tag pinned makes it a standing memory.

Write discipline. Writers call ctl know add; code enforces the hygiene. If the normalised content hashes the same as an active entry's, or it shares ≥ 85% of its words with an active entry on the same topic, the write confirms that entry instead of adding a copy: confirmations go up by one, and confidence closes half the gap to 1, capped at the new evidence's source prior plus 0.05 harness/knowledge.py:140-191, 247-259. Every write returns up to three related entries (same topic or ≥ 35% word overlap), so the writer sees a likely contradiction while it is still one entry. A content change creates a new version that supersedes the old one, and a wrong entry is retracted with a reason; nothing is deleted. The prompt adds the rest: write "one self-contained statement that names the item, place, NPC or spot … search finds entries by their topic and content, so an entry that leans on context you had at the time is lost", label guesses --source inferred, and scope character-specific entries docs/OVERSEER.md:457-472.

Retrieval. Word search came first. On 09-30 embeddings were left out on purpose: "FTS5 + stemming is enough at this size and needs no model or network" c0bf3ce:docs/MEMORY.md. Three days later it had stopped being enough: word search missed paraphrases ("my character died" against "resurrection"), and the table had just taken in 820 Discord facts. Relevance became hybrid on 10-03 f55bc2c; docs/PLAN.md:686-707. A query is embedded with bge-small-en-v1.5 [28] (384 dimensions, local, on the GPU) and compared by cosine with a vector of "topic: content" for every active entry. Separately, FTS5 ranks entries by BM25 [20], with the topic weighted 3× and tags and entities 2×. The top 60 of each ranking are fused by reciprocal rank [8] and scaled so the best candidate gets 1:

rel(e)=f(e)maxe′⁡f(e′),f(e)=∑r∈{cos,BM25}160+rankr(e)
(3)

Candidates are then reranked the way Generative Agents ranks memories [18], a sum of relevance, recency and importance, with two terms added for confidence and location harness/knowledge.py:351-374:

score=rel+0.4e−ln⁡2⋅aged/14+0.5importance10+0.3conf+0.6max⁡(0,1−d∞40)
(4)

Recency halves every 14 days, and its age counts from the later of the last update and the last access, so retrieving an entry also makes it recent. Importance and confidence are the write-time values. Nearness applies only when the caller passes a position: d∞ is the Chebyshev distance in tiles to the entry's location on the same facet, and the bonus fades to zero at 40 tiles. Every returned result counts as an access. Vectors live in knowledge_vec, keyed by a SHA-1 of the model name and the text, and the searcher embeds whatever changed before each search. Writers (the proxy, ctl know add, the Discord promoter) therefore never load the model. A sidecar vector database was rejected as "another file to back up and keep in sync for ~1k rows that numpy scans in microseconds" docs/PLAN.md:696-700. On a copy of the store, loading the model took 0.56 s and a hybrid search over 4,107 vectors 0.18 s on the desktop GPU; a ctl call costs about 1.5 s in all, mostly process start and model load measured on the copy; docs/PLAN.md:704. When the running Python lacks the embedder, recall falls back to BM25 and says so (recall: words).

The brief. ctl know brief builds the start-of-shift context without a query string. It returns three disjoint lists for the character being played: pinned (every pinned entry, in full, uncapped), standing (unlocated procedures and preferences of importance ≥ 7, capped at 12), and relevant (entries within 40 tiles, entries whose entities name a mobile in view, and entries whose cosine with the current intent, open junctures or task is at least 0.65) harness/knowledge.py:423-470. The 0.65 floor and the exact-name match replaced a looser design on 10-04. The old brief embedded one query made of every mobile's label, and at the guild house a stablemaster's label called up the Shelter Island stablemaster's prices at cosine 0.70 docs/MEMORY.md "Situational brief".

Calibration. search has no similarity floor: it always returns its top results. The prompt therefore teaches the Seer to read the cosine, "around 0.6 and up is on topic; below ~0.55 is noise" docs/OVERSEER.md:438-441. On a copy of the store, "what is the capital of France" peaks at cosine 0.54, and the pinned guild-library procedure (importance 8) still comes back first.

What the store holds. At the snapshot the table has 4,107 rows: 3,715 active, 366 superseded and 26 retracted (Table 10). It is mostly imported. 3,388 of the active entries (91%) are community facts from the Discord pipeline and 173 more are official ones stored as doc. The Seer's own observations number 116, the owner's directives and corrections 27. The two groups also differ in the ranking inputs (Figure 14): Discord facts are capped at importance 6, almost all sit at 2–4, and their confidence is 0.65–0.85; the Seer's and owner's entries sit mostly at 5–9 with confidence 0.85–0.95. All 62 located entries are the Seer's or the owner's, so the nearness term helps only them. 49 entries are scoped to a character.

A worked example. At 20:21 on 10-05 a Seer playing Character Omega asked its memory "finish a lumber trip by hand convert logs to boards" (chat #2855). Table 11 shows the ten results the Seer got back, with the score taken apart term by term. We re-ran the same search on a copy of the store with the clock set to that moment.

The example shows three properties of the ranking that we had not designed for. First, fusion compresses relevance. Ranked first in both lists, an entry gets 2/61; tenth in both, 2/70, which scales to 0.87; first in only one list, 0.5. All ten results here have rel between 0.74 and 1.0, while the prior terms (rec + imp + conf) differ by up to 0.3 among them. In the full re-run, across the 60 entries ranked, relevance spanned 0.26–1.0 and the priors 0.67–1.14. The most relevant entry (#118, rel 1.0, the highest cosine) came fourth, behind two entries with higher importance.

Second, the priors favour the store's own entries. Importance, confidence and location are all higher for what the Seer and the owner wrote, so imported facts lose ties. The third most similar entry overall is a community fact (cosine 0.748) that ranks 17th. In a re-run of "my character died, how do I come back", the most similar entry is a community procedure for resurrection after dying in the wilderness (cosine 0.759). It ranks 14th, behind the Seer's account of Character Omega's death at Wintertop and the owner's resurrection procedure. For a Seer that is supposed to treat Discord facts as "leads, not truth", this bias may be what we want; it was never measured.

Third, scope is enforced in one path only. brief drops entries tagged for other characters; search does not harness/knowledge.py:311-349 vs 440-466. So the top two answers to a question about Character Omega's trip were Character Delta's lumber goal and banking routine from 10-01, both on Shelter Island. The other eight came from the first two days of play. The Seer got a stale, partly foreign context and had to filter it by reading.

How it was used. Every ctl know call except stats also posts a chat row of kind memory, so usage is on record. By the snapshot there were 365 such rows: 149 adds, 137 searches, 30 briefs, 21 gets, 19 updates, 8 confirms and 1 pin SELECT json_extract(data, '$.op'), count(*) FROM chat WHERE kind = 'memory'. These include calls coding agents made while testing, which we cannot separate. Six of the rows came after 2026-10-05 20:30, around the character's two later deaths, and show the store doing its job: at 20:43 on 10-05 the Seer looked up the owner's resurrection procedure (#4095) and its own entries on an earlier death and a nearby healer, and at 10:15 on 10-06 it searched "how do I come back after dying healer resurrection", walked 212 steps to a wandering healer and accepted the resurrection gump chat #2864-2866, #2972-2975; world death events 10-05 20:42:59, 10-06 10:14:37. Only 9 entries have ever been confirmed (5 observed, 2 community, 2 doc). The Seer retracted one entry, its own duplicate, and no Discord fact. The design assumed the Seer would confirm or retract community leads as play tested them; in practice that loop barely ran.

Finding

There was no retrieval evaluation. No labelled set of questions with expected entries exists, so we report no precision or recall figures. The unit tests check the mechanics on toy entries (deduplication, versions, the location boost, and a fake three-axis embedder under which "dying" meets "resurrect") harness/test_knowledge.py. The only quality evidence is what the logs show: the calibration probe, the cases above and the access counts. The 10-04 changes to the brief (the 0.65 floor, character scoping) came from the owner's complaint that most of a brief did not apply to Character Omega and from one bad live match, not from a metric.

5.6Importing community knowledge

Most of the knowledge table was imported. A read-only capture records the pages the Outlands Discord web app itself loads while scrolling, at a reader's pace: about 10k messages an hour 22a8047, 97k in all docs/PLAN.md:93. Raw chat is "unreliable: jokes, outdated patch info, wrong answers", so only vetted facts reach the Seer (Figure 15). The pipeline is memory ingestion with provenance: each promoted entry carries source_type community (or doc for official posts), the tag discord and a reference to its fact id and a jump link to the message.

A claim survives only if it cites message ids and quotes one verbatim. The adjudicating model proposes a fact and verdict, but code recounts independent authors: official needs an official-channel claim, consensus at least two supporting authors outnumbering dissent, else single_source or disputed, and confidence is "a fixed function of the final verdict … not the model's opinion". Promotions are capped at importance 6, below standing-brief level. The first run (10-03) promoted 820 facts for $26.26 over 761 calls; the rebuild (10-04) took 20,053 grounded claims to 14,016 clusters and 3,561 active entries for $71.11 over 1,953 calls, list-price estimates on the owner's subscription.

The pipeline also keeps the store consistent over re-runs. Promotion state is kept per target database, so a trial run into a copy never mixes up the real store's ids. An entry the Seer retracted or superseded is never re-added, even under new wording. When a fact's verdict drops, the pipeline retracts the entry only if it added it and nobody has confirmed it since docs/PLAN.md:668-674. At the snapshot the 3,561 are still there: 3,388 consensus facts as community and 173 official ones as doc. The 3,102 rows of the 10-04 promotion arrived between 12:00 and 12:45 and grew the store by 10 MB (Figure 16).

5.7Memory as a bus and as training data

A durable bus. The Seer, the runners, the viz and the Telegram bridge never talk to each other directly. Runners post junctures, everyone posts chat rows, and meta holds the running tasks, a heartbeat and one cursor per consumer (§9.2). Since there are no queues, only rows and cursors, any party can restart alone, and every message stays on record. That is how the paper can report median acknowledgement times per juncture kind, and how this chapter can count memory lookups.

Labelled data. The store doubles as a data set. Laya's fine-tuning set took its 221 real player lines from speech_heard events, read through a mode=ro connection harness/triage_data.py:23-25, 151-153 (Table 18). Every speech hold that ends in a clear writes a speech_clear job event with the lines, their context, Laya's check and direct scores and how long the hold lasted. At the snapshot there were 53 such rows, every one with a Laya score, and each is a real verdict on a real line. They are labels waiting for a use: the current training set does not read them (§9.8). The planner's training data is the trip rows. Ten committed captures are test fixtures, the viz replays captures through the same ReplayDriver as memory.py ingest, and most charts in this paper are read-only queries over the store.

5.8Operating it: backups, handoff, growth, cost

Since 2026-10-01 an hourly scheduled task copies the store to the NAS with the SQLite online backup API from a mode=ro connection: it never checkpoints or writes the live file, yet includes the WAL's rows. The copy is switched to a rollback journal so it stands alone, checked, gzipped and deduplicated by sha256. That day's restore drill matched all 11 tables row for row (247,502 events) docs/NOTES.md "Backups".

On 2026-10-04 the owner wanted to "play on a desktop for a while and find its changes on the laptop afterwards." dbhandoff.py keeps one holder and numbered generations on the NAS: push uploads a verified snapshot as generation N+1 and releases it; pull installs it and records the holder. Two checks make it safe. The writer check: PRAGMA journal_mode=DELETE on a WAL store succeeds only for the sole connection, so push refuses while anything else has the store open, even a read-only reader. The fork check: a per-table fingerprint (row count plus sha256 over rows in rowid order; 1.15 M events in 1.9 s) is compared with the one recorded at the last sync, so a pull never silently overwrites local changes. The very first desktop pull refused, "this store has unsynced changes", because a harness command had created an empty database first da0bcb9. Opening the store writes to it, so the empty file already counted as local history.

Lesson

A live store on the network share was rejected because WAL needs every connection on one host; sync clients (OneDrive, Syncthing) were rejected because they would copy harness.db and its -wal at different moments and tear the store. Merging diverged stores would collide autoincrement ids in eight tables. In the plan's words: "Preventing forks is cheap and merging isn't, so forks are refused."

Growth. Figure 16 shows how the store filled. Event volume follows time in game: 641,252 events on 10-05, the busiest day, which ended with a lumber shift until 23:40; 532,419 on 10-03; 91,315 on 10-04, the day of the move to the desktop; and 195,322 on 10-06 up to 12:00. The hourly backups show the file growing from 52 MB on 10-01 at 23:00 to 342 MB at 11:00 on 10-06: about 6.5 MB per hour between 10:00 and 20:00 on 10-05, 11 MB per hour during the evening shift (20:00–23:00), and under 1 MB per hour overnight, when the log took in little but keepalives. Gzip shrinks it 5.5 times. Knowledge grew in two steps, the two Discord promotions; everything the Seer wrote itself fits in a few dozen rows a day.

Reading a live store. Every database number in this paper was read from a store a runner was still writing (§10.8). Three rules made that safe. Connect with mode=ro, because the harness's own connect() writes the schema on open. For anything heavier than a count, take a consistent copy with the backup API first. And cut every count at a timestamp rather than "now". The knowledge searches in this chapter ran on such a copy, because a real ctl know search updates access statistics and would have changed what it measured.

Cost. Storage: 352 MB for six and a half days, 157 MB of it the JSON payloads of events, a fifth of those keepalives. Compute: local embedding, a fraction of a second per search plus the model load. Money: the two Discord runs, $26.26 and $71.11 at list price on a subscription. The rest is engineering time. memory.py, knowledge.py, embedder.py, dbhandoff.py and backup.py come to about 2,000 lines, and docs/MEMORY.md was touched by 26 commits (Appendix B).

5.9Lessons for AI engineers

1. Keep one append-only record and derive the rest

We stored every event before we knew what we would need. Guard points were backfilled from events recorded before their table existed, hatchet wear was read from journal events, Laya's real negatives came from speech events, and this paper is mostly a set of queries over the same file. The price was a log in which 29% of rows are keepalives. A single SQLite file with IF NOT EXISTS schema growth and JSON payload columns took seven schema additions in six days without a migration.

2. Record failures with the same care as successes

A trip row written only on success made the dangerous spots look good. After the row moved into finally, 45 of the 68 trips that recorded an outcome turned out to be aborted ones. When code learns from its own history, the logging path is part of the model.

3. Check the scale of every term in a reranker

Reciprocal-rank fusion squeezes the relevance of good candidates into a narrow band (0.5–1.0), and additive priors for importance, confidence and recency then decide the order. In our store this demoted imported facts systematically and put an earlier character's preferences first. Recency that counts from the last access also feeds on itself. None of this is visible without taking scores apart on real queries, and a small labelled query set would have been cheaper than finding it in a paper.

4. Enforce provenance in code; give curation an owner

The Discord import worked because code, not the model, decided what counted as evidence: substring grounding, author recounts, confidence fixed by verdict, an importance cap. The curation loop that was left to the agent, confirming or retracting community leads as play tested them, hardly ran: 2 confirmations, no retractions, and 93% of imported facts never retrieved. A memory that only grows needs a process that prunes it.

5. Prefer ground truth you can read over memory you have to learn

Walk memory was the harness's first planner and failed the first time the character came out upstairs. The client's own map files replaced it within an hour. Learned memory earns its place where nothing can be read (regrowth, yields, hazards, prices, who our pet is), and the LLM's memory where judgement is needed. Neither should stand in for data the system can read directly.

6The lumberjack loop

Chopping wood was the first job the agent learned end to end. One hand-played demonstration was mined into facts, and those facts became a deterministic runner. The runner leaves home, chops at script pace, answers the shard's CAPTCHAs, holds for anyone who speaks to it, comes back through a house steward and stores boards. Every live failure became an offline scenario test.

6.1Goal and hard constraints

The brief in docs/LUMBER_LOOP.md is short. The agent should learn the loop, run it and improve it: chop trees, recall home, enter the rental room, convert the logs to boards there and store them. The plan, committed on 2026-09-29 at 18:05 8b4291c, fixed a division of labour that held all week. We learn by demonstration and run a deterministic routine. An LLM is called only to compose, repair or reflect. The optimizer works only inside constraints that are not optimisation targets:

  • CAPTCHAs go to the human by default, with an auto-solve toggle since 10-01 (§6.7).
  • "Pacing is a floor, not a knob": no tightening of jitter, walk pacing, breaks or the daily cap.
  • No speech except "guards" after a guard flight. No packet a stock client wouldn't send.
  • On Shelter Island, never renounce Young status, so no travel there at all.

Three characters ran the loop: Character Alpha (Test Shard: Shelter 09-29/30, Horseshoe Bay 09-30 after the owner renounced Young), Character Delta (a fresh Young character: Shelter 10-01/02, overworld from the afternoon of 10-02 to 10-03, plus a short 10-04 session) and Character Omega (the Guild, from 10-04). The runner, harness/loop_lumber.py, is 3,550 lines at the snapshot commit ee59524. The planner that picks its spot and trip size is described in §7.

6.2Learning by demonstration

A loop like this hinges on numbers nobody can guess: serials, gump and button ids, cliloc message numbers, the order of menu clicks. Exploring live to find them costs CAPTCHAs and deaths. So at about 20:42 on 2026-09-29 the owner played one full loop by hand through the proxy (session 20260929_204225). "Nothing in the harness injects during the demonstration; the proxy only relays and records."

Cliloc: a numbered localized message. The server sends 1010018 and the client shows "What do you want to use this item on?" from Cliloc.enu.

loop_mine.py timeline replays a capture through the proxy's own SessionTap. It prints walks collapsed to "N steps", clicks, lifts, drops and cursors, gumps with their button ids, rendered clilocs and per-container amount changes. It ends with every serial acted on and the packet ids it could not parse. By 21:03 the demo had become harness/data/loops/lumber.json, pinned by test_loop_demo.py 39330c9. Among the facts:

  • One attempt per use. Double-click the hatchet, get cliloc 1010018 and a cursor, and target a tree. About 4.1 s later the server answers with fail cliloc 500495 or "You chop some logs and put them in your backpack."
  • 1 log → 1 board, both at 0.025 stones, so the runner converts once per trip, just before storing.
  • A 60 s travel lockout after leaving the room (41.5 s of walking plus a "must wait 19 seconds"). The deed quantum is 5,000.
  • The real CAPTCHA (gump id 0x00000001) came with a buttonless decoy on every attempt. That shaped the detector (§6.7).

Extracting them automatically before seeing a demo would mean guessing at their shape; after the demo they're read off the timeline.

— docs/LUMBER_LOOP.md §4, 2026-09-29

The demo was tiny: 12 attempts at Lumberjacking 60.2, 2 successes, 12 logs, one attempt per ~9.5 s. It was enough. Eighteen minutes after the mining commit the runner and its offline end-to-end test were green 0e22e17.

Some facts were cheaper to fetch by sending the overseer. On 2026-09-30, 09:18 to 10:25, it ran four "Young demos" through ctl while the owner watched (docs/missions/YOUNG_DEMOS.md). Hatchet 0x… went from 483 to 477 uses over 19 attempts and 6 successes. That means one use per successful chop; failures and conversion are free. The overseer also read vendor price lists without buying, closed a moongate gump to stay Young, and died on purpose in the New Player Dungeon to learn how resurrection works. It surfaced seven harness gaps, all fixed that day (§9).

6.3The runner as a state machine

Since 2026-10-04 e5345b9 a trip starts in the rental room, or within NEAR_LANDING = 60 tiles of the home landing (Figure 17). The runner restocks, mounts, checks for a live trapped pouch and the Harvest Aspect armor, goes out, chops stand after stand, then comes home to convert, store and restock. The pre-emptions make it a machine rather than a script. A CAPTCHA hands off and resumes the same attempt. A creature triggers a walk-away of ESCAPE_RUN = 20 tiles, at most three per trip. A player at 2 tiles triggers a keep-away to 4. Three things end the trip at once with a recall home: a red (murderer) player in view, the trapped pouch popping (a thief at work), or low hit points. These escapes, shaded red in the figure, end the run. Since 2026-10-05 21:24 bddc446 a run whose escape recall lands home still goes into the rental room, converts and stores before it stops (before, about 1,380 logs sat unconverted at the landing after one shift of such stops), and since 2026-10-06 11:49 ee59524 that last room phase ignores everything but players and death, because a PK's spell cast before the recall can still land at home. The room can refuse entry for 2 minutes after PvP docs/LUMBER_LOOP.md:675; then the logs stay in the trapped pouch until the overseer takes them in. A plain abort away from home also recalls home and stores first, so a run never ends standing in the field 5589433. Each trip writes its episode row in a finally block.

6.4Skills, not prompts

Under the states sit deterministic controllers: goto, smart_harvest(spot), convert_logs, enter_room, store_in_container, exit_room, plus deed skills that are designed but unbuilt. They generalise errand_bank.py, the Phase 3 acceptance task that walked to a banker and back. Every skill has preconditions, a success check against world-model evidence, a timeout and a typed failure. They share agent_link.py. Link talks to the proxy's ports and respects the agent gate. Mover plans 3-D routes (§4), charging 4× for a tile holding a mobile.

Decision

The LLM picks skills; it does not run the loop. It is called at start, on a typed failure the routine can't handle, and afterwards for reflection, so a steady-state cycle costs 0 API calls. We rejected an LLM per cycle ("nothing to decide in the steady state") and deferred Voyager-style LLM-written skills [25] docs/PLAN.md.

6.5The harvest attempt and Smart Harvest

Until 2026-10-04 each attempt aimed at one tree static from the map. The runner walked a planned order of trees and moved on at "depleted" (500488/500493). On 10-04 at 12:12 b3d9f0d the owner switched it to Smart Harvest: target yourself and the server chops a nearby tree that still has wood. The runner's answer is byte-equal to the stock client's in capture 20261001_214649:

6c 00 <cursor> 00 0020f127 <x> <y> 00000000 00000190
# our serial, our x/y/z, our body graphic (0x0190)
# "The z must be movement's: the world model's self z said 10
#  there while the client sent 0."

The docs call it "a simplification, not a detection fix", because there is no tree to aim at and fewer walks. The unit of work became the stand. next_stand plans walks to within 1 tile of the 6 nearest trees, preferring stands with more trees in reach. It stays until "You do not see any harvestable resources nearby." The store's 1,142 stands averaged 2.99 attempts and 20.5 logs, with a median stay of 18.2 s.

SMART_RANGE = 1 is "the only value the evidence proves". Every stand had a tree at distance 1, so the server's true reach is still unmeasured.

The share of attempts lost to "move on" answers did not change (Figure 18): 25% depleted per tree before, 25% nothing-nearby answers after (counted per answer, not per tree marked). Successes rose from 41% to 64% of attempts, but that is confounded. Omega's skill went from 50 to 95.6 under the Harvest Aspect, and the early era includes Shelter's halved odds (§10).
