Failures fell with the skill: 31 failed chops against 1,725 successes since 2026-10-05 20:30 CDT inferred.

6.6Chop pacing: from human to script

The first runner chopped like a careful person. It used lognormal delays (0.95 s median to aim, 2.2 s between attempts), a 12% per hour fatigue drift, hesitations and fidgets, under the doc's rule that "the agent only ever gets slower or less direct". On 2026-10-04 the owner overruled that rule for the harvest cycle alone:

every harvester on the shard runs a script

— the owner's decision, 2026-10-04, docs/LUMBER_LOOP.md §13

The cycle now runs at a Razor script's pace (humanize.SCRIPT_MEDIAN): hatchet ~0.2 s after the reply, cursor answered ~0.1 s after it appears, no fatigue. Stashing the last chop's logs moved inside the server's ~4.2 s chop, 0.8 s after the target, because a lift 0.47 s after the click drew "You must wait to perform another action." Walking, menus and the room keep their human texture. Live that evening e82df6c, target-to-target time fell from 9.36 s (62 cycles) to 4.92 s (39), with the server's reply at 4.17 s both times. In the doc's words, "the cycle is now the server's chop time plus ~0.75 s".

6.7The CAPTCHA solver

Harvesting raises a CAPTCHA every 5–10 minutes: a dialog with a three-digit number and a box to type it into. Three wrong answers block harvesting for 6 hours, and the shard can also read response time and long-run accuracy as detection signals ANTICHEAT.md §3, §8.8. So a wrong answer costs far more than a slow one, and the design follows from that. A human answers by default (the runner pauses and beeps), the solver sits behind a toggle in the viz header, and the solver is allowed to refuse. This subsection describes the solver for readers who want to build one: what the input looks like, the algorithm, how it was labelled and evaluated, and where it can still fail.

Finding the real CAPTCHA among decoys. Every lumberjacking attempt also opens a decoy dialog that carries the CAPTCHA's words ("Captcha", "Type the Value") under a fresh random gump id, with no reply button and flags that keep it off the screen. The human never sees one and the stock client cannot answer one, so any reply to a decoy can only come from automation inferred: a honeypot for bots that match on text ANTICHEAT.md §8.13. The store holds 7,552 of them at the snapshot (2026-10-06 12:00 CDT), none with a reply button, and the harness's audits found no reply to any. The real CAPTCHA is gump id 1, with text entry 2 (at most 3 characters), a Guide button 1 and one more reply button, the submit, whose id changes with every CAPTCHA (594, 843, 528, 606, …). The first detector keyed on 594 and missed the second CAPTCHA it ever saw. Detection now requires gump id 1, text entry 2 and exactly one reply button other than Guide, and never looks at text harness/captcha.py:78-85.

The input is a point set, not an image. The digits are not pictures. Each digit is drawn as 9–18 tilepic elements, small item graphics placed at explicit layout coordinates, so the gump packet itself lists every dot position. The graphic changes from CAPTCHA to CAPTCHA (35 different ones across the 67 real CAPTCHAs) and carries no information. The digit is the arrangement of the dots, which are displaced from a fixed shape and sometimes include strays (Figure 20, left). Reading a digit is therefore classification of a small 2-D point cloud, and there is nothing to OCR. The plan had a screen-crop classifier or a small CNN in reserve in case the glyphs ever came as pixels ANTICHEAT.md §8.8. With 7 labelled CAPTCHAs (21 digits) when the solver was built, a nearest-neighbour matcher over point sets fit the data better: it needs no training, its decisions can be inspected one reference at a time, it can say "not sure", and each new labelled CAPTCHA adds three references with no retraining.

The algorithm harness/captcha.py:

  1. Segment. Collect the tilepic coordinates (at least 18), sort them by x and cut at the two largest gaps in x, which gives three clusters. Each cluster must pass sanity gates (6–25 dots, a height of 40–120 px, a width of at most 120 px; the 67 real ones have 9–18 dots, 62–84 px and 32–102 px). Anything else is not treated as a CAPTCHA.
  2. Normalize. Centre each cluster on its centroid and divide by its height, so position and size drop out but width and slant stay: p~=(p−p‾)/h.
  3. Compare. Measure the distance from the cluster A to each reference B with a symmetric, trimmed Chamfer distance, minimized over small translations. This is chamfer matching [2] [3] on point sets, made robust to outliers in the manner of the partial and modified Hausdorff distances [14] [10]:
    D(A,B)=minδ∈Δ⁡ 12[T0.85{minb∈B⁡‖a−b−δ‖}a∈A+T0.85{mina∈A⁡‖a−b−δ‖}b∈B]
    (5)
    T0.85 is the mean of the smallest 85% of the nearest-neighbour distances, and Δ is a 9 × 9 grid of shifts within ±0.09. Chamfer distance needs no one-to-one matching of dots, which matters because the dots are displaced and their count varies. Trimming the worst 15% in each direction ignores strays, and the shift search absorbs the centroid error that strays and missing dots cause harness/captcha.py:97-115.
  4. Classify, or refuse. The cluster takes the digit of its nearest reference among the 79 in the font, at distance D1: nearest-neighbour classification [9] with a reject option [6]. Let D2 be the distance to the nearest reference of any other digit. The margin
    m=D2−D1D2
    (6)
    must be at least 0.09 for all three digits, or the solver returns nothing and the human gets the CAPTCHA harness/captcha.py:118-142. The margin is Lowe's ratio test [16] with a threshold of 0.91 (m≥0.09⟺D1/D2≤0.91), taken against the nearest other digit rather than the second-nearest reference. That difference matters: two references of the same digit agreeing is not ambiguity.

Each digit costs 79 references × 81 shifts in pure Python, about a third of a second on the desktop, so about a second per CAPTCHA, hidden inside the deliberate human-paced delay described below.

Labels from the server. Labelled data came for free, because the server says whether an answer was right. harness/captcha_mine.py replays session captures, pairs every real CAPTCHA gump with the 0xB1 answer to it and the server's "Captcha successful." within 10 s, and keeps only accepted answers. Their three clusters become new references. Before adding anything, it reports whether the font as it was would have solved each new CAPTCHA, and with what margin, so every addition first serves as an out-of-sample test harness/captcha_mine.py:1-21. The dataset grew from 7 CAPTCHAs on 09-30 to 26 on 10-03 (12 sessions); the font has 79 references, 78 real plus one synthetic 0, with 4 to 15 per digit.

Evaluation. Table 12 lists every test, from weakest to strongest evidence. Grouping matters in the held-out test. Digits from one session tend to look alike, so the test holds out whole sessions, not single digits. A leave-one-digit-out test would have been optimistic.

What the gate does and does not do. The margin protects against ambiguity: a cluster that lies about as close to a 3 as to an 8 is refused. It does not protect against novelty. The 10-01 failure shows the difference: a 9 unlike any reference was simply nearer to an 8 than to anything else, by a comfortable margin. This is the open-set recognition problem [23], which every nearest-neighbour classifier has, and the defences against it here are outside the classifier. First, the font grew from real data: the second real 9, which the owner called "real funky" (86 px wide, with strays on both sides), was read right out of sample at margins above 0.6, and with it 194 reads correctly. Second, a human answers by default. Third, a rejected answer is noticed: the server opens a fresh CAPTCHA, the solver reads that one, and after its third rejection it hands over (--captcha-max-strikes 2 counts the rejections it carries on after) harness/loop_lumber.py:1768-1808, 3464. Three rejections are also the shard's block threshold, so this last line of defence leaves no slack; it has never been tested, because no answer was ever rejected. The digit 0 is the open case. Its only reference is a synthetic oval ring, because none of the 201 digits seen so far was a 0. If the shard drew digits uniformly from 0–9, the chance of that would be 0.9201 ≈ 6 × 10−10, so it almost certainly draws from 1–9 inferred, and the synthetic 0 has never been tested.

A synthetic score that fell as the solver improved. The 0.09 gate was set on the jitter test: with the first 21 references it accepted 99.2% correctly and refused 12% harness/captcha.py:17-24. Each later batch of real references lowered that number, to 98.1% with 37, 97.2% with 73 and 96.98% with 79, while every real out-of-sample test improved. Real digits vary more than the synthetic jitter does, so a jittered reference lands closer to other digits' real shapes as the font fills up inferred. On 10-03 the test's bar was lowered from 97% to 96%, and the real-data tests became the ones that count ANTICHEAT.md §8.8 "Dataset 26".

Answering like a person. A reading is not sent at once. The runner waits a lognormal delay with a median of 11.5 s (σ 0.38, stretched 12% per hour of play), chosen from the owner's measured solves of 7.7–17.5 s. It then checks that the client has not answered meanwhile, so one gump never gets two answers, and sends the stock 0xB1 with every text entry filled as the client would. Finally it waits up to 12 s for "Captcha successful." or a fresh CAPTCHA, which counts as a strike harness/humanize.py:52; harness/loop_lumber.py:1768-1808. Figure 22 shows the whole path.

The outcome. 67 real CAPTCHAs, 67 answers, 67 “Captcha successful.”, 0 strikes. The solver answered 57 (3 on 10-01, 11 on 10-02, 43 from 10-03 on, every one after 10-03 15:24) with a median of 13.23 s from gump to answer; the owner answered 10 with a median of 10.21 s. By design the solver is a little slower than the person it imitates.

Lesson

Four things carried this solver, and none of them was model capacity. The input was read from the protocol instead of the screen, which turned OCR into point-set matching. The model was one that can refuse: a nearest-neighbour vote with a margin, whose every decision can be traced to a reference. The server labelled the data, and each new label was first used as an out-of-sample test. And the evaluation that counted was real and grouped by session, while the synthetic benchmark drifted the wrong way. The margin handles ambiguity, not novelty; the policy around the solver (a human by default, a strike budget) is what handles a digit it has never seen.

6.8Staff: an alarm that has never rung for real

Staff are the one encounter the agent must not handle alone: “a player unresponsive to a GM for ~2 minutes while gathering is jailed, then banned on repeat.” Since 09-30 anyone speaking nearby holds a harvest job until a human or the overseer acks 38c427d, and staff hints in that speech raise gm_suspected with a repeating alarm 021bcec. Since 10-01 a local model, Laya, scores every held line and raises the alarm at once when a line looks like an attendance check (§9.8). On 10-04 the owner suggested a GM is probably an invulnerable player, so sight alone should alarm. Notoriety 7 alone would have fired in 12 of 13 lumber sessions, mostly on player vendors; notoriety 7 with flag 0x20 had never been seen (Table 13) 8e9cff7.

No staff_sighting exists in the store, and no staff alarm has fired since 10-02. A GM shown blue or grey, or hidden, would still get past the sight rule, so the speech hold remains the backstop.

6.9The home trip

Storage moved three times. The first home was the Shelter inn room, entered by saying room. From 2026-10-01 the boards went to the bank instead (no rent, no Test Shard wipe) a29b7b1. On 10-04 at 19:15 storage went back to a room e5345b9: "the room is the safe place: no one follows in, no recall reaches it". The logs get converted away from the grove; a 12 s conversion under attack in the field had cost 45 hits the day before. There is also no speech and no banker search, and Omega co-owns a room whose exit lands at the guild house.

Out is the door's "Exit to House Steward", a teleport to the landing at (withheld). That teleport starts the 60 s lockout and the Stationary Penalty, and both are walked off before the first chop. From there the runner recalls "as close to the lumbering spot as we can via rune tomes in the rune library or our own rune tomes/books" (the owner's rule; the landing choice is in §7). Home is always the default rune of Omega's own runebook, "Guild Loot Chest". Power words to arrival took 1.95–2.09 s over 34 live recalls harness/escape.py. At home the runner finds the house steward and walks its menu, "Room" → "Visit Other Rooms" → the owner's row. room.py never presses End Rental Contract.

In the room the logs come out of the hue-38 trapped pouch of the thief guard (§8). Omega sets it off himself, takes one hit, and converts each stack (one try per stack plus 3 retries; since 2026-10-06 the runner and the overseer's ctl act convert share this flow in harness/convert.py 89130d8). Since 2026-10-05 the boards go into the Resource Stockpile ("It is where we will now drop off all our boards", the owner). Since 22:19 that evening the runner targets each pouch holding boards once, which adds every stack in it ("You add 2 item(s)" for two stacks, live), and only a loose stack on its own; never ourselves or a bag of supplies, which "would add every valid item" in it. The stockpile path sets off no pouch; only the old chest path still does 1038b59; harness/stockpile.py targets. After the chest's boards moved in, it read 8,693. Restock and Resupply at the room shelf then return the spent pouch, and "Omega keeps exactly the loadout". The first live trip of this design (10-04, 22:06–22:17, Horseshoe Bay) chopped 209 logs at 11 stands in 527 s and stored 240 boards (with 11 logs from the aborted first attempt and Harvest Aspect doubles). It then took 9.5 s to enter the room, 14.7 s to convert and 4.1 s to store.

6.10Testing from captures

test_loop_lumber.py (3,237 lines at ee59524) puts the real proxy in front of a simulated server. The simulator speaks the demo's packet shapes and the room's captured menus, and a scripted "human" answers CAPTCHAs. It serves decoys on every attempt, one solver-readable and one unreadable real CAPTCHA, a door that swings shut and moongates whose renounce prompt must be closed. The main run's two trips assert the invariants. The agent goes out by the door and in by the steward. It replies only to the CAPTCHA, gate prompts, runebook and room menus. It sends no speech at all, and every log not stolen ends up stored.

The working rule was that every live incident becomes a scenario that fails against the old code. The suite now holds 22 end-to-end scenarios, each in its own process with private ports, up to 8 in parallel (about 2 min critical path, 10 min serial). It also holds 14 unit checks, some of which replay live captures through the world model with no simulator (Table 14).

6.11Failures and pivots

The first evening alone brought four live attempts and four fixes. The overworld deaths behind later entries are in §8.

  1. 2026-09-29 21:23Lost upstairs. The room exit dropped Character Alpha on an inn's upper floor, where 2-D walk memory failed after 21 blocked moves. The owner's directive, "the full x/y/z Outlands map", produced the map decode and pathfinder within the hour.
  2. 2026-09-29 22:10NPCs as walls. Two NPCs in a hallway made all 8 trees "unreachable". The owner noted that "in UOO you shove through mobiles", so mobiles became a cost rather than a wall.
  3. 2026-09-29 22:27First full trip: 46 boards stored, after fixing vendor range and a random CAPTCHA button id. Run 3 stored 50 boards in 8 min 25 s, about 355 logs per trip-hour.
  4. 2026-09-29 23:04Chopping from a cave. The agent stood at z −20 under trees at z 5. The server allowed it, but "a player in that cave can't see or click a tree on the surface". Goals became height-aware.
  5. 2026-10-02Survivorship bias. Only trips that reached the bank had been recorded, which "flattered exactly the spots where trips get cut short". The episode row moved into finally.
  6. 2026-10-04Smart Harvest, the room again, script pace. Two false alarms followed. The Harvest Aspect's proc effect was read as a spell on us, and a new run saw the previous run's own pouch pop as a theft.
  7. 2026-10-05A day of fixes. The Wintertop death, a stuck conversion, bad landings, aggro zones, the stockpile and Restock. Each fix came with a scenario.
  8. 2026-10-06No run ends in the field. The overnight shift added 23 trip rows (13,851 logs, 12,623 boards stored). A world save delayed a recall past its arrival wait, the run exited at the landing and a snow elemental killed Omega 15 s later; since then an abort away from home recalls home and stores first, and an escape's last room phase ignores a PK's spell landing after the recall ade127e, 5589433, ee59524.

Lesson

The demonstration bought exact ids; it could not show other floors, crowded hallways, caves under trees, monsters or thieves. Each of those gaps surfaced live, got fixed once and was pinned by a test.

7Self-optimization: where to chop and how much to carry

The runner works one spot; a pure-function planner decides which spot, how many logs per trip and which hatchet, using a small Bayesian model of place, character and danger, a renewal-reward trip size and Thompson sampling. In its latest snapshot it is deliberately exploring: no spot has more than a 3.0% chance of being the best, and nearly every trip is sized by the grove, not by the hazards. Appendix D collects the notation and the derivations, with one spot worked through by hand.

7.1Objective and architecture

The objective: boards stored at home per agent-active hour, net of expected losses docs/LUMBER_LOOP.md:177. One log makes one board. Pacing is a floor, not a knob: the optimizer picks places and trip sizes but never tightens the delays, breaks or daily cap that the runners' pacing rules fix.

harness/lumber_opt.py (1,613 lines at ee59524; first commit 5a33805, 2026-10-02 23:26) is a pure function plan(...) over plain lists, fed by plan_from_store. It returns one runner command, e.g. ctl run lumber --spot witcher_244 --trips 1 --logs-per-trip 3970 --regrow-min 65 --timeout 9924, so "the overseer, a future daemon or a human run the same decision" docs/PLAN.md:488-489. The Seer (§9) asks ctl lumber plan before each run. It does not always run the pick: during the Seer6 shift of 2026-10-05 small explore groves gave 262–392 boards a trip, so from run 14 on the overseer ran the greedy spot instead, with the pick's trip arguments and --spot docs/NOTES.md:816-824 (ec339a1), and the 2026-10-06 morning shift did the same (chat: "Greedy pick: seek ye witcher_40", "seek ye witcher_23, the greedy grove"). Since 89130d8 (2026-10-06 10:03) the plan also carries the greedy spot's own run, and --exploit makes the pick itself greedy.

7.2Spots, recency and the character

A spot is only a place: an area, its trees, a PvP flag and a hazard_prior. Since 2026-10-04 every trip starts and ends at home, so getting there is not part of it. Evidence is weighted by recency, so shifts in competition, killers or patches show up within weeks:

wi=0.5agei/14 days
(7)

Place and character are modelled separately. Character Omega's Lumberjacking rose from 50.1 to 95.6 in about a day and a half (§10), so a plain per-spot average would favour whichever spots were visited last. The success chance per attempt follows the wiki, summed over the ten wood colours a tree can be:

A hatchet's material and quality add a tool bonus that multiplies the chance: Exceptional +0.04, Bronze +0.08, Avarite +0.18 docs/LUMBER_LOOP.md:81-82.
p(S,b)=min⁡(1, ∑jbasej100clip[0,1]⁡(S−offj′divj′(1+b))),j′=j if S≥minj, else ordinary
(8)

S is skill, b the tool bonus, basej the chance a tree is wood j (81.75% ordinary to 0.25% avarwood); a colour above our skill counts as ordinary, an inference the code flags harness/lumber_opt.py:337-356. It checks out: Character Delta at 69.1 hit 44/63 at Terran (0.70) against 0.69 predicted docs/NOTES.md:362-364. Each trip's chopping time tc is rescaled to today's chance; walking is not:

Hadj=max⁡(F−tc+tcpthen/pnow, 0.1F),Hadj≥0.25 h for a place failure
(9)

with F the field time. The floor makes a trip the place spoiled (no reachable tree, a town region) cost a quarter hour at zero logs, so a dud spot loses its optimistic prior harness/lumber_opt.py:499-510. The Harvest Aspect (armour that sometimes doubles a yield) is left to recency weighting.

7.3Field rate and overhead

The field rate λs is logs per field hour, walking between trees included. Logs come in lumps (7.92 per success over 4,125 successes), so trips scatter far beyond Poisson; a quasi-Poisson dispersion ϕ (Pearson χ2/dof over trips of 3+ minutes, floor 8) was 14 on 2026-10-02, 26.8 on 2026-10-05 20:26 and 17.0 at the snapshot harness/lumber_opt.py:725-742. Discounting the evidence by ϕ:

λs∼Gamma(α0+1ϕ∑iwiLi,  β0+1ϕ∑iwiHadj,i),α0=μ2/s02,  β0=μ/s02
(10)

The prior is empirical Bayes: μ is the mean rate of spots with half a weighted field hour, s02=max⁡(sample variance, (0.35μ)2), and 1,200 logs per field hour before any data harness/lumber_opt.py:825-838. An unvisited spot is "a spot like the others", explored but not trusted. Tree density was rejected as a prior term ("it didn't predict logs per field hour across the 7 spots with trips"); it returns as capacity.

Overhead T is everything but chopping. Its prior, in seconds:

T0=10⏟room exit+0.45(library walk+walk in)+2⋅4⏟recalls+60⏟lockout+15⏟into room+40⏟convert, store
(11)

The posterior is a weighted Normal counting the prior as one observation; the per-trip spread is floored at 30 s and the posterior sd is that spread over n, so it can fall below 30 s harness/lumber_opt.py:704-722, 857-862. Overheads are short: 102 s at Horseshoe Bay, 139 s at witcher_23.

7.4Three ways a trip ends early

The rewrite of 2026-10-03 (86075f3) split danger into three competing hazards per field hour, each a per-spot Gamma posterior over weighted exposure, shrunk to a pooled rate:

  • Death hD: nothing stored, every unblessed item lost, plus an inferred R=20 minutes of recovery.
  • Sent home hS: a recall escape, guard flight or creature stop (§8); the load comes home.
  • Theft hT: a thief takes a share f∼Beta(1,1) of the load and the trip goes on.

Deaths are rare, so their prior is built from commoner events: hostile sightings per field hour σs, times a pooled π=P(death|sighting), plus a pooled creature-death rate hC:

hD∼Gamma(10m0+∑w⋅died, 10+Es),m0=σsπ[pvp]+hC,π∼Beta(1+pkw, 3+seenw−pkw)
(12)

Es is weighted field hours. A death counts against a spot if it falls in a trip there or within 30 minutes after ("the Terran PK killed us 11 s after the runner stopped") harness/lumber_opt.py:517-551, 892-915, 1119-1126. Prior strengths are in Table 15. The same PK deaths count twice: in the pooled π prior and in the spot's own death count harness/lumber_opt.py:869, 894-895, 1119. That empirical-Bayes double use makes hD at the death spots (Terran, witcher_23, witcher_282, witcher_196) somewhat overconfident while deaths are this few.

7.5How much to carry: from a square root to renewal-reward

On 2026-09-29, before the first live trip, we set the return trigger with a textbook inventory argument, the economic-order-quantity trade-off [13]: at r logs per minute, overhead T and death hazard hD, the cost per stored log is

cost(Q)=rTQ+hDQ2r+hDTback⇒Q∗=r2T/hD
(13)

The rule's hazard is death only, "PK encounters × P(death)" docs/LUMBER_LOOP.md:190: being sent home loses nothing, so it has no place in a cost per stored log, and with hD+hS the rule would give sizes of 288–646. Its flaws, named at the rewrite: it credited a dying trip with Q/2 banked, its expected deaths hDQ/λ exceed 1 on long trips, and Q sat on a 60-minute stint cap docs/PLAN.md:501-504. The replacement treats a trip as one renewal-reward cycle [21] (Figure 26). Chopping Q logs takes tf=Q/λ; with h=hD+hS and theft thinning the load at k=hTf:

C(t)=λ(1−e−kt)k,B(Q)=e−htfC(tf)+hS∫0tfe−htC(t)dt,PD=hD∫0tfe−htdt,𝔼[time]=T+∫0tfe−htdt+RPD,Rate(Q)=B(Q)−supplies−GPD𝔼[time]
(14)

G is the gear at risk (unblessed items at replacement price); it and the supplies are priced in logs at the board price. Every integral has a closed form, so PD≤1 for any Q; that is why "a clamp on deaths" and Monte Carlo per Q were both rejected docs/PLAN.md:509-510. best_q scans 41 log-spaced sizes from 200 to 10,000 logs plus the weight cap, then refines by golden section to 10 logs harness/lumber_opt.py:797-822.

Finding

The square-root rule was not far off. At the snapshot's means its Q is 7–24% below the renewal-reward optimum (Horseshoe Bay 2,281 vs 2,950; witcher_23 2,793 vs 3,510; Terran 1,260 vs 1,350; witcher_291 1,227 vs 1,610), which costs at most 0.12% of the rate in our recomputation. The rewrite fixed the accounting, not the size: at Q∗, P(death) per trip is 3–9% but P(sent home) is 69–91%. Threats, not deaths, end most long trips.

That shapes the curves: being sent home costs only the next trip's overhead, so "being sent home alone never shrinks Q (nothing is lost); deaths, thefts and the gear at risk do" docs/LUMBER_LOOP.md:336-337. On the 2026-10-03 store the rewrite changed sizes by up to ×1.6 on eligible spots (×2.2 on the Young-only Shelter spot), mostly by lifting them off the stint cap, and net rates fell as sent-home stops were charged honestly docs/LUMBER_LOOP.md:395-407.

7.6Grove capacity and regrowth

The owner's point on 2026-10-03: a sparse grove dries up sooner, so its trip pays full overhead for fewer logs. The runner ends a trip dry once its listed trees are chopped, so a trip holds at most

grove_logs=avail×ψ×Ltree,ψ∼Beta(10ψ0+y, 10(1−ψ0)+n−y),ψ0=∑y+1∑n+2
(15)

avail counts tree tiles not depleted, unreachable or marked out of wood within the regrowth window, y of n tried tiles ever yielded, and Ltree is 19.3 logs per tree cycle, pooled over 471 cycles (17.7–20.2 per spot) harness/lumber_opt.py:622-689. The yielding share ψ varies, 0.47 at witcher_282 to 0.86 at corpse_creek at the snapshot (0.46 to 0.85 on 2026-10-03), and the model matched dry trips (Horseshoe Bay ~677 predicted, dry at 605 and 613). When the cap binds, the run is one trip, and the runner gets the uncapped Q∗ "so it chops until the trees really run out instead of stopping at the estimate" (aa1de12).

Regrowth comes from pairs of a depleted answer followed by a later try on the same tree. A pool-adjacent-violators isotonic fit [1] gives P(regrown|gap); the window is the first block reaching 0.6, rounded up to 5 minutes harness/lumber_opt.py:578-619. It replaced a 20-minute guess that "sent the runner to depleted trees".

Since Smart Harvest (2026-10-04) the server picks the tree, so new data adds no regrowth pairs or tried tiles harness/lumber_opt.py:585-587, 631-634.

The estimate is biased upward by design: "Retry gaps shorter than the window in use are no longer observed, so the estimate can only move up from here unless the window is shortened on purpose" docs/NOTES.md:359-361.

7.7Choosing a spot: Thompson sampling

Thompson sampling [24] [22] picks by drawing from the posteriors. For each eligible spot the planner draws (λ,T,σs,π,hD,hS,hT,ψ) once, takes maxQ⁡Rate over every other grid point, and the best draw wins. Repeating this 2,000 times gives each spot's P(best); the pick is labelled explore when it is not the best by posterior mean harness/lumber_opt.py:1215-1228, 1259-1261. The theft share f and the creature rate hC are not drawn: both enter the mean plan and every draw as pooled posterior means harness/lumber_opt.py:908-915. Spots are ineligible for 30 minutes after a death or player threat, 20 after a thief, until regrowth after a dry trip, and 7 days after two place failures in a row.

Decision

Thompson sampling "explores in proportion to how likely a spot is to be the best, needs no tuning constant, and varies the routine". Rejected: ε-greedy ("explores bad spots as often as promising ones, needs an ε schedule"), UCB ("deterministic, so the same spot order every day; a fixed pattern is a bot signature") and an LLM reading the stats ("not reproducible, no uncertainty accounting") docs/PLAN.md:482-489.

Variation is required, not an inefficiency to remove.

— docs/LUMBER_LOOP.md §6, "Anti-pattern guard"

Discovery. ctl lumber discover turned three seed spots into 132. It counts trees in 29×29-tile windows on a global 7-tile lattice within 200 tiles of each Witcher rune (a public library of 360 wilderness runes, 359 table ids plus a duplicate 83; §4) with a summed-area table, ranks windows across runes, and keeps those with 25+ trees, a walk of at most 300 tiles and distance from towns and guard points harness/lumber_opt.py:1467-1596. The first search looked 21 tiles out, and "212 of 360 runes had too few trees". On 2026-10-03 the owner approved all 125 candidates not named after monsters at once: "heavy exploration is the point of the Thompson sampler" docs/PLAN.md:520-537.

Landing. A trip recalls to the rune nearest the grove that has a walking route in, from the home library or our own books, skipping monster-named runes, the "Bad Places" tome and remembered bad landings harness/lumber_opt.py:194-211. The owner's rule: "always recall as close to the lumbering spot as we can … never public moongates or starting at banks and walking".

7.8Hatchets, wear and the price of a board

Each hatchet we own or could buy at a known price rescales the rate through the chopping share ρ of field time, minus wear at one use per success:

λ′=(ρλpnowp(b)+1−ρλ)−1,value=v−vlogs/success⋅priceuses⋅1gp/log
(16)

where v=maxQ⁡Rate(λ′), with a bought hatchet's price added to G harness/lumber_opt.py:1023-1039. One use per success was measured twice (a hatchet went 500 → 163 over 337 chops on 2026-10-05). Wear is small: an iron hatchet (25 gp, 500 uses) at 1,700 net logs per trip-hour costs about 11 gp, 0.4 logs, per hour. The bonus is not: the exceptional, mastercrafted bronze hatchet Omega was handed on 2026-10-05 (+0.16; docs/NOTES.md:578-584) lifts p at 80.1 skill from 0.776 to 0.900, about 11% more logs per field hour at a 0.7 chop share. Every carried hatchet is lost on death, so a bought one is "worth it where nobody can kill us, not where they can". Unpriced hatchets get a break-even price instead.

Gold becomes logs at board:ordinary: the wiki's 9.5 gp until 2026-10-05, when the lowest commodity ask put it at 26.8 gp (134,000 gp per 5,000-board deed), and coloured woods were mostly no dearer (dullwood 22, copperwood 20, bronzewood 19; only shadowwood, at 30 gp, beat ordinary). When those commits landed on 2026-10-05, revaluing the 63 trip rows of the time at the asks instead of the wiki's 9.5 gp took their 16,036 logs from 147,773 to 428,442 gp (ba7ade5, b2238c7); that basis prices logs without a wood breakdown as ordinary, while §10 values only the logs with one. For the planner, gear and supplies got cheaper in logs: a 200 gp recall charge is 7.5 logs, not 21.

7.9A snapshot of the planner

We ran plan_from_store from ee59524 read-only on the store as of 2026-10-06 12:00 CDT (no live character, cached routes, seed 1). Skill from the last trip row was 95.0 (p=0.913, no tool bonus without a live character); pooled π=0.132, creature deaths hC 0.040 and sent home 2.98 per field hour, thefts 0.014 (prior only), regrowth 65 minutes, rate prior 3,166 logs per field hour (CV 0.35). The creature rate is a posterior (prior 0.01/h over 20 pseudo-hours) that still counts only D11 of the five deaths Omega has had on lumber trips since the morning of 2026-10-05: D9 was read as a PK, and D10 and the two later ones (2026-10-05 20:43 on a witcher_268 trip, 2026-10-06 10:14 on a witcher_23 trip) fell 59–64 tiles from their spot's centre, outside the 54-tile attribution margin; raw, that is 1 attributed creature death in 9.8 field hours.

132spots (123 eligible, 37 with a trip)
0.030highest P(best), an unvisited spot
117 / 123eligible spots grove-bound
≈87%of P(best) held by never-visited spots

The pick was witcher_244, explore, P(best) 0.009: its grove holds an estimated 422 logs, so one trip with an uncapped quota of 3,970, about 11 minutes, 343 boards expected, P(death)=0.012, P(sent home)=0.33. The greedy best, witcher_23 (net 2,959 logs/trip-h at its grove-capped Q; field rate 4,008 logs per field hour over 8 trips), has P(best) 0.001. With 94 eligible never-visited spots sharing a prior wide enough to reach the best measured rates, the sampler spreads its bets thin; on 2026-10-05 Omega went to a new spot on 20 of 27 trips (§10), and the overnight and morning shifts ran the greedy spot instead (above). Visits measured less than they suggest: 37 of the 132 spots had a trip (38 with Shelter Island, no longer a spot), but only 23 of the 37 have any field time. The other 14 had only trips that ended before chopping, keep the prior 3,166 [1,856–4,640] and hold P(best) like unvisited spots, while the well-measured spots (Horseshoe Bay, Terran, witcher_282, corpse_creek, witcher_291, witcher_280, witcher_265) all have P(best) = 0. And trip size is now set by the groves, which are smaller than Q∗, not by the hazards.

Caveat

Much of the danger model is still prior: the one observed theft (10-03, Player T) was never booked as a theft event, and none has been booked since (0 theft events at the snapshot), so hT and f are pure prior, and R and the room terms of T0 are guesses. One aborted trip is a false hazard sample, a Harvest-Aspect sparkle read as a spell docs/NOTES.md:602-607. The snapshot is not a live plan either: without a proxy the gear at risk is the last row's hatchet (now the exceptional bronze one, unpriced, so G=0) and its tool bonus is left out of p (0.913 instead of 0.974 at 95.0 skill), and only cached landing routes count.

8Staying alive

The harness never fights a player, so survival is a matter of noticing early and leaving fast. This chapter shows how it tells a player killer from a goat, how the escape grew from “stop” to a recall that recasts until it lands, and how each of thirteen deaths became a rule within hours. It also covers the thief guard and the one runner that is allowed to fight. The CAPTCHA solver and the staff alarm, which keep a harvest job going rather than a character alive, are part of the lumberjack loop (§6.7, §6.8).

13character deaths, 09-30 → 10-06 (3 to one player killer)
12 / 14player-triggered escape recalls landed (both failures Bastet, old 3-try code)
0deaths in 36 hunt-runner visits (173 kills)

8.1The stance: never fight back

Notoriety is the colour of a name: blue innocent, grey attackable or criminal, orange enemy, red murderer, yellow invulnerable (code 7). A PK (player killer) is a red who kills other players for their loot. See §2.

The threat research of 2026-09-29 opens with one rule: “The harness never attacks a player.” Hitting a player brings Heat of Battle, which blocks recall (the one fast way out), makes you criminal and draws staff attention docs/research/THREATS.md §0. Everything below is detection and evasion, never retaliation.

The data for that evasion came partly from accidents and partly on purpose:

Let's bank what we've got and go somewhere potentially more dangerous and see if we can get PK'd or killed by mobs for science (data to improve our agent harness)

— the owner, viz chat to the overseer, 2026-10-02 17:27

Two hours later a red named Bastet killed Character Delta in the Terran wilds, and the owner replied by phone: “that's exactly the data we were hoping for”.

8.2Reading a mobile: the threat classifier

Outlands gives no clean “this is a PK” signal. Monsters show grey, mongbats turn criminal, human-bodied NPCs exist, and a pickpocket is blue until he steals. threats.assess() is a pure function of one state snapshot, so it can be unit-tested and replayed over captures harness/threats.py.

identify() decides what a mobile is, in order: a ghost is ignored; notoriety 7 is an NPC; mobile flag 0x20 or a “(Young)” label makes a player; a non-human body named “a/an …” is a monster; a “Name the title” label is an NPC; a human body with a creature name and no flag is a monster at notoriety 3 (the orc-hunter fix, 0add311). Any other human body counts as a player. The 0x20 flag is an empirical find: by 10-04 it was on 1,474 human mobiles at notoriety 1/3/4/6 and never on 2,607 notoriety-7 sightings or about 2,400 non-humans docs/PLAN.md "Staff alarm".

Movement turns Chebyshev distance into an arrival estimate, ETA=max⁡(0,d−rs)⋅s, with s = 0.2 s/tile for a player running, 0.1 mounted and 0.4 for a monster, and strike range rs = 12 tiles for a player (an assumption: RunUO's spell range; the Outlands value is unsourced), 1 for a monster. The flee radius is the distance at which a recall still lands first:

Rflee=rs+⌊trecall+tmargins⌋
(17)

The design example, a 4 s recall and 1 s margin against a red on foot, gives 12 + 25 = 37 tiles, past the 18-tile view, “so any visible red means flee”. The deployed runner uses a 2 s recall and 1 s margin: 27 tiles against a red on foot, 42 against a mounted one.

Creatures are judged by aggression: swinging or casting at us, war-mode flag 0x40 unless the body or name is on a passive list, known aggressive bodies, else not aggressive. That default changed on 09-30 after lumber trips stopped for a walrus and a goat c7dc39c.

Damage was harder than it sounds. “Outlands has never sent one with us as the defender”: all 3,645 swing packets (0x2F) in the store at the snapshot (2,172 when this was found on 10-03) are our own, so the live damage signal is the hits trend. Spells are caught by their visual effects on us or by lines such as “Magic reflect removed.”; all 93 such signals in the captures came with an attack. Since the server never names an attacker, hit_attackers blames adjacent creatures first, then ranged ones in reach, then anything within 12 tiles.

8.3Bastet, three times

The same red killed Character Delta three times in 24 hours, and each encounter broke a different assumption (Figure 31).

Terran wilds, 10-02 19:43. Bastet rode into view at 18 tiles. The runner aborted at 0.29 s and then stood still: its only response to danger was an Unsafe stop. “Bastet is attacking you!” came at 2.80 s; the first hit at 4.58 s carried a hamstring (no running for about 3 s); five hits and 102 damage later Character Delta was dead at 10.96 s. The “5…1” countdown over Bastet's head was most likely an explosion-potion fuse inferred: a blast followed 1.2 s after “1”, after the death: “Weapon, not explosion.” Tracking never fired, and the runner's ETA guess of 0.6 s was eight times too pessimistic docs/NOTES.md "Bastet".

That last number flipped the design. The one live runebook recall on record took 2.09 s from button to arrival, and Bastet needed 4.58 s from sight to first hit. “So a recall started within ~2.4 s of sight lands before the first hit. … A recall is the only action with a chance, so it wins.” Recall-on-sight shipped at 22:16 that night f7aab09.

Nusero, 10-03 18:04. Bastet appeared at 11 tiles carrying the Stationary Penalty, which suggests he had just recalled in or had stood hidden inferred. The new escape reacted fast, starting a recall at 1.05 s, but his Weaken landed at 1.88 s and broke it. The instant retry was refused as “not recovered”, his Harm broke the third try, and the three-try escape gave up at 3.64 s. Then nothing hit Character Delta for 4.5 s (Bastet's potion blew on his own tile, two swings missed), and no escape was running to use it. The verdict: “A mage PK who recalls onto us beats a 2 s recall escape”.

The commit and NOTES say Bastet “struck 5.5 s later” after the tracking hit. The DB event clock gives 6.51 s to “attacking you” and 7.59 s to the first hit. We suspect the note was rounded from a different anchor.

Terran wilds again, 10-03 19:08. This time Tracking reported “Bastet (55 spaces to target)”, but the react range was 40 tiles, so it was only logged. He came into view 4.57 s later, during the chop's 2.1 s aim pause. The runner answered the chop cursor first and opened the tome 2.5 s after sight; the first hit at 3.02 s broke the cast, and Character Delta died at 8.39 s. The real bug: “The runner was blind inside every pause and result wait”, because Human.wait was a plain sleep c4db365. The owner first asked by phone for a 60-tile react range; offered 40, 80 or any by the agent, he chose 80 4017175.

8.4The escape, v1 to v3

The escape (harness/escape.py) presses the default rune's charge in the runebook or rune tome and falls back to casting Recall. It was rebuilt twice, each time from measurements.

v2 (10-03 18:27) came from a study of the casts in the store docs/research/SPELL_INTERRUPTS.md. Recall takes a median 2.03 s from power words to arrival (1.95–2.09 s, 27 casts). Creature melee breaks a cast 44% of the time (26/59), damage-over-time ticks never (0/13), Bastet 3/3. After a disturbed cast, all 30 live retries fit RunUO's pre-AOS recovery rule, where e is how far into the cast it broke and T the cast time:

trec=max⁡(0.2,1−e/T) s
(18)

So v2 has no try limit, only a 20 s budget, and presses each retry the moment recovery ends. Replayed on Nusero, the old code gives up 2.73 s after the double-click (live: 2.72 s); the new one lands at 5.0 s d6e6c63. “A PK has to land a fresh interrupt within every 2 s cast, and giving up hands him the time.”

v3 (10-05) learned the failure that killed Character Omega at Wintertop, “This book needs time to recharge.”: a recharging book is now answered by casting Recall on the book itself, which worked live at 10:59 87b53fe. On 10-06 a world save held a recall's landing to 5.18 s, past the 5 s arrival wait; the retry failed and Omega died at the landing (D13), so the arrival wait now runs at least 10 s past our power words ade127e.

In the store, 31 of 34 logged lumber escape recalls landed: 30 by book charge, 2.09–2.20 s from press to arrival (median 2.13 s), and one by Recall cast on the book. Two of the three logged failures were Bastet, under the old three-try code; the third was D12, a monster read as a grey player, whose one cast was disturbed 1.4 s in. D9's escape failed before a cast (a recharging book) and is not in that count. Of the 14 escape recalls a player triggered, 12 landed; a pk_escape juncture is written only after a successful escape, so the twelve such junctures (five of them reds that Tracking reported at 35–64 tiles, four on 10-05 and one on 10-06) are clean by construction memory DB job_events recall, junctures. The newest player escape shows the limit of “landed”. On 10-06 at 11:38 a mounted mage with bonded pets came into view under a blue name, spoke the words of Explosion 3.1 s later and turned grey 3.9 s after that, 5 tiles off, with “… is attacking you!”. The runner pressed the book 0.38 s after that notice and landed home, but the delayed blast went off on Omega just after the landing (100 → 69 hits) docs/NOTES.md, ee59524. If a recall fails off guarded ground, a guard flight runs A* to guard points learned from “now protected” notices at the tile where they appeared 4cb8b9c.

8.5Thirteen deaths and what each one bought

Figure 32 and Table 16 list every death, near-death, theft and costly false alarm up to 2026-10-06 12:00 CDT. The memory store holds 12 death events; the thirteenth, Character Alpha's planned demo (09-30 10:18), is in a stored session but predates the death event. Three were Bastet, three the overseer acting by hand, five monsters on or just after runner trips, one a blind long walk, one the demo. 10-03 alone had five.

The overseer deaths taught the bluntest lesson. At Urukton Bluffs the recall-in had knocked Character Kappa's arcane staff into his pack; the overseer walked about 85 steps into an orc room and fought bare-fisted for 2 damage a blow while losing about 6 hit points a second.

Yeah no manual fights in dungeons is a good rule. An LLM is way too slow to react for combat.

— the owner, omp session, 2026-10-03 20:31

Lesson

Early on, false positives cost trips: a walrus, a goat, a battle trainer. From 10-05, false negatives were killing Omega: an unknown failure message, a house door in an escape route, an 8.93 s humanizing pause, a monster read as a player, a landing delayed by a world save. Each fix made the runner more cautious; lumber flee events rose from 2–13 a day (09-30 → 10-04) to 44 on 10-05 (10 more on 10-06 by noon), the price of the owner's final policy: “run and recall until home, never stopping in the field”.

8.6Thieves: step away, and a trapped pouch

At 100 Stealing a thief takes about 200 logs per grab, once every 5 s, from 1 tile away. The one we met, Player T, was blue until the instant the reagents left the pack (T1). The owner's summary, “thieves look friendly to us until they steal, and so a friendly player being within 2 tiles of us AT ALL while we're lumbering is almost certainly a thief”, became the 2-tile rule 2516411. Attacking him is out, so the guard has three layers ad5a6c0:

  1. Keep-away. The runner pauses as if reading, then walks to ≥ 4 tiles: “One step beats the 5 s steal cooldown, where a 2 s recall would still leave them in reach.” If he closes again: recall, and a 20-minute cooldown on that spot.
  2. Trapped pouch. Logs go into a trapped pouch after each chop. Its pop was decoded from our own set-off (hue 38 → 0, an explosion effect, a sound, −1 hit) a929050; one of our own pouches going off when we did not open it is an alarm, while an explosion sound alone is not, since it can be someone else's pouch or a spell 5e70fad. “A pouch is a delay plus an alarm, not a lock.”
  3. Ledger. Losses become theft events that feed the optimizer's theft hazard (§7).

Live, keep-away fired twice on 10-05, both for mounted blues at 2 tiles. Neither came closer and nothing was stolen; we suspect passers-by. Both pouch alarms so far were false: F2, and F3 on 10-06, when a PK's Explosion going off at the home landing sounded like a pouch. T1 is still the only theft, and it was never booked as a theft event.

8.7The one runner that fights: hunt loop and crawl

After the overseer let Character Delta fall to 2/96, fighting moved into a deterministic runner, loop_hunt.py f5008fd. Each tick it takes the first of Leave → Speech hold → Heal → Stationary Penalty → Loot → Fight → Idle that applies. It leaves for a hostile player within 12 tiles, for two or more attackers below 80% hits, or below 60% plus a margin for the walk out, and heals with a potion when it can, else by spell.

The Stationary Penalty is an Outlands debuff: it appeared 301.0–314.8 s after the last step in all 40 measured cases, and 5 steps clear it.

One fight spot yields only 0.4–0.5 kills a minute and invites the Stationary Penalty, so the crawl patrols the New Player Dungeon instead ee62f02. Its floor graph has 10,829 tiles, up to 182 route steps deep, cut into five depth zones with 147 waypoints. Zone 1 starts at the store's measured 23.4 hits lost per minute; each deeper zone's prior is the one above times a depth risk of 1.5; and a zone opens only when its predicted damage is at most 30 hits/min. Since 23.4×1.5=35.1>30, zone 2 stays shut until zone 1 proves cheaper than about 20 hits/min.

Across 10-02 and 10-03 the hunt runner made 36 visits (265.7 minutes) for 173 kills and 2,785 gold. It left 32 times (18 for low hits, 9 for multiple attackers, 5 done) and died 0 times. The crawl has run live in zone 1 only.

8.8What still kills us

Nusero set the open problem: a stealthing mage who appears at 11 tiles and casts within 1.9 s beats a 2.03 s recall. docs/PLAN.md "PK survival" lists three answers. Detecting stealthers: Character Delta's Tracking sees hidden players only within about 8 tiles. Magic Reflection: at Nusero it would have bounced the Weaken, and recall 1 would have landed 0.49 s before his Harm; Character Delta lumbered with it up on the evening of 10-03, when it absorbed a gazer larva's spell (N3). Mounted flight with scripted healing helps only with a guard zone or line-of-sight break in reach. None has met a real PK yet. The 10-06 mage showed a milder form of the same problem: his power words under a blue name triggered nothing until his attack notice, and a spell already cast followed the recall home. The system survives the threats it has met, and it learned each one by dying to it first.

9The Seer: an LLM on the outer loop

The language model never plays the game. It sits one loop out: it wakes on a database row, reads the situation through a JSON command-line tool, picks the next deterministic runner and handles the exceptions.

9.1From an API daemon to an agent that waits

At 17:08 on 2026-09-29 the owner chose a standalone Python loop on the Anthropic API for the agent runtime ("this is our own harness after all"), choosing skills and never raw packets session log 2026-09-29; docs/PLAN.md:59, committed 17:10. It lasted six hours. At 23:21 the owner sent a ten-point bedtime brief whose first point replaced it:

Tasks stay programmatic but an agent oversees them, and can get awoken at important junctures… we could keep using omp (Oh My Pi, this coding harness) and just make a CLI… not sure how we'd 'yield' back to the AI at important junctures in that case.

— the owner, 2026-09-29 23:21

The answer, committed at 23:47 49d433d: an omp session drives harness/ctl.py, the SQLite store is the bus, and the yield is ctl wait, a blocking call run as a background shell job. The daemon was "rejected for now" and could later replace omp on the same bus docs/PLAN.md:190-191.

The brief's first sentence stuck. Chopping, walking, fighting and storing are deterministic runners with their own guards, because "an LLM in the inner loop would be slow, costly and harder to keep stock-identical" docs/OVERSEER.md §1. The overseer reacts in a poll (~1 s) plus a model turn; anything that can't wait tens of seconds belongs to a runner. We learned it twice anyway. On 10-01 the overseer's improvised fight loop let Character Delta fall to 2 of 96 hit points among mongbats, and a programmatic hunt task replaced it that night f5008fd. On 10-03 a subagent fought by hand in Urukton Bluffs; the recall cast had knocked Character Kappa's staff out of his hands, and he died 15 s after one manual act attack, swinging his fists.

Decision

"Never fight by hand in a dungeon (user decision 2026-10-03): an LLM reacts far too slowly for combat … In dungeons only ctl run hunt fights; you scout, choose where it runs and watch." The same goes for lumbering: the Seer runs the planner's command verbatim, because "hand-picked arguments spoil the data" (§7). From 22:43 on 10-05 the goal was boards, not exploration: on Seer6's proposal the main session told it to take the planner's greedy (best known) pick instead of its explore pick, passing the pick's other arguments with --spot IRC to Seer6, 2026-10-05 22:43; docs/NOTES.md (ec339a1), and on 10-06 at 10:03 ctl lumber plan gained its own greedy run command 89130d8.

Figure 33 shows the control plane.

9.2The juncture bus and ctl wait

The bus is three tables in harness.db. junctures(id, t, source, kind, severity, summary, data, acked_t) is what runners want the overseer to know; chat holds the conversation (kinds message, thought, action, memory); meta holds tasks, cursors and a heartbeat. There are no queues, only cursors, one set per consumer, so each is restart-safe alone.

Runners post threat, pk_escape, captcha, death, speech_nearby (the job holds until acked), gm_suspected (a staff alarm repeats until acked) and rarer kinds; the task wrapper posts task_done/task_failed. ctl wait polls once a second and returns on an open juncture above its cursor with severity ≥ attention, on any task end, on a new user chat row, or when its timeout runs out, at most 20 events per wake harness/ctl.py:107-109. The "any task end" clause was the first bug of live use: on 09-30 an info-level task_done didn't wake the overseer, which "sat idle after its trip" until a fix landed about four minutes after the task ended, two minutes after the owner noticed b264824. The coding agent told the stranded overseer through the bus itself, with an ad-hoc notice kind.

task_wrap.py removes a finished task from meta.tasks before posting its juncture, so a woken overseer can start the next run at once. While a run is on, the prompt has the Seer wake every ~150 s (ctl wait --timeout 150) to read the status and the task log docs/OVERSEER.md:496-497, since 7a48fd5; only an idle Seer makes no tool calls and spends no tokens between junctures, with the shell job finishing as the interrupt.

9.3ctl as the agent's API

Every overseer move is a ctl subcommand that prints one JSON object and exits 0 iff ok (Table 17). The guard rails live in the API, not the prompt: act accepts 29 whitelisted names and refuses raw packets, any act while a task runs, the captcha gump and button-less (honeypot-shaped) gumps. attack targets only hostile monsters, never below 30% hits; buy is capped at 50,000 gp a day. Free-text speech is allowed only during a speech_nearby hold, at most 120 characters, and must pass a regex that refuses words like bot, script, ai, proxy, claude or test harness/ctl.py:96-101. Every act mirrors a stock client gesture and is logged as a chat action.

Most of it grew on demand. The first live overseer, on 09-30, kept reporting "ctl has no …" and would not work around its rules: "I'm not allowed to edit the harness myself; I've asked the main agent to add an unequip/equip act to ctl. Holding still here until it lands." Each gap became a commit that day. Asked to farm gold by killing monsters, it declined under its no-attack rule; the owner overruled it within a minute, and the new policy was committed about five minutes later a0d78f7.

9.4The prompt and the persona

docs/OVERSEER.md §5 is the operating prompt, and with 95 commits it is the subsystem's most-edited file (ctl.py has 73). On each wake the overseer thinks a reading of every event, follows a per-kind table (task end → next planned run; failure → retry once; possible staff → ctl alert first; captcha → don't touch), acks, and records what it learned. Since 10-03 shifts are continuous, ending only on the owner's word, a death, possible staff or a bug.

Hawkwind is the seer at Lord British's court in Ultima IV (1985) who tells the Avatar how far they have come in each virtue.

The voice arrived on 10-03 in four commits in 33 minutes: Lord British calling the owner "Avatar" (14:45), the display name "the Seer" (14:48), Hawkwind who "reads the signs" (15:15), and Hawkwind's actual lines, verdict then direction (15:18) 1eaef1d → 1cf2217. The owner: "oh yes, The Seer is very good." A fifth commit fixed person-mixing ("First I bank the logs, then seek ye…") with a strict second-person rule 40b2873. He is "blunt and exclamatory, not mystical", and never speaks in the game, where speech stays "lowercase, short, human".

A misfortune! Bastet (red, mounted) slew Character Delta at terran_wilds (874,1480) at 19:08, 1070 logs into a 1160-log trip…

— the Seer, harness.db chat #2031, 2026-10-03

9.5Memory in a shift

The Seer remembers through the store, not through its context. A shift opens with ctl know brief, which returns every pinned entry plus the standing procedures and whatever is near or in view; before a decision the prompt asks for one plain-language ctl know search; and what the Seer learns goes back with ctl know add, with a source and an importance. The knowledge table, its hybrid retrieval and its ranking, the Discord facts that make up most of it, and what the logs show about how well it worked are in §5.5.

9.6Shifts in practice

14overseer shifts, ≈ 47.9 h
377junctures posted
3,021chat rows, 2,033 of them actions
0real staff contacts recorded

Splitting overseer chat rows at gaps over an hour gives 15 windows and about 47.9 hours in seven days (to 2026-10-06 12:00 CDT); one window is a single memory lookup, which leaves 14 shifts (Figure 34). The windows include some ctl calls coding agents made while testing. The first, at 09:18 on 09-30, ran the owner's Young-character demos on the Test Shard.

What woke the overseer changed with the work (Figure 35): on 10-01 mostly speech holds, and on 10-02 more speech holds than anything else; from 10-03, out in the wilderness, threats (with run failures) dominate. Median acknowledgement times: 6.2 s for speech holds, 14.9 s for threats, 21.3 s for failures, about 5 minutes for deaths. Captchas, acked by the runner once solved, have a median of 11.1 s, which is really the owner's solve time.

Overseer subagents had already run the 09-30 demos and the 10-03 NPD quest. At 15:18 on 10-03 the owner made them the rule for lumbering: "You should probably start an overseer subagent and tell it what to do, since when you pause for long times leaving Character Delta in the wilderness he's liable to get killed." From then on named Seer subagents played while the main session engineered and relayed over IRC; on 10-04 the owner typed no chat rows at all, and on 10-05 two, after looting Character Omega's corpse harness.db chat, 10-05 20:44–20:46. The first five Seers of 10-05 started 27 runs for Character Omega, stored 8,156 boards, took Lumberjacking from 53.1 to 80.1 and lost him three times. Seer6 (20:14–23:39) then ran 15 runs and stored 8,033 boards, the most of any shift, taking Lumberjacking to 90.5 with one death (a norse bear rider at the Norse Settlement landing, 20:43); after explore picks gave 262–392 boards each, it switched to the planner's greedy picks for the owner's goal of boards. Seer7, on the morning of 10-06 and still running at the cut, ran 9 runs, stored 4,590 boards, reached 95.6 and lost Omega once, to a snow elemental at the witcher_23 landing (10:14) episodes 99–122; docs/NOTES.md (ec339a1). Costs are in §11.

The Seer was good where judgement over data mattered. It logged every run's pick and death risk, overrode a risky explore pick ("Prudence: seek ye horseshoe_bay instead", p_death 0.034 vs 0.021), refused a grove with a tracked red near its landing, and reported runner bugs with log lines while holding the character safe; Seer4 and Seer5 found the runner's tree ping-pong in the task logs and reported it, the first time within a minute of the owner. Reports from the 10-05 evening and 10-06 morning shifts turned into fixes the same way: Seer6's open items (no ctl act convert, no command for the planner's greedy pick) became 89130d8; Seer7's report of a run where Omega stood still while losing hits led to bounded escape routes 87bbcab, and its landing death to a longer wait for a delayed recall arrival ade127e and a rule that an aborted run recalls home and stores first 5589433. It was bad where speed or self-awareness mattered: it fought by hand, began answering a stranger's "did u do all this" that the owner judged suspicious, until the owner killed the agent, and never noticed the viz lag; the human watching the map did.

9.7The operator's side: viz, Telegram, supervisor

The viz is a React page fed by viz_server.py, which polls the proxy's state port ~4 times a second and never touches its control port. Its rule is parity: "If the human can't see something, neither can the agent, and vice versa." A top-down map over the decoded terrain sits in the centre; beside it, the Overseer panel shows the owner's lines as royal-blue cloth and the Seer's messages, thoughts, actions and memory items as ink on parchment. On 10-05 the map showed Character Omega "bouncing between trees for minutes after he had recalled home": a closed-gump leak had grown states to 1.8 MB, each SSE client had a 20,000-frame FIFO, and in a replay a reader limited to 1.5 MB/s fell 147 s behind after 200 s. One newest-state mailbox per connection brought states to ~170 KB and lag to ≤ 0.1 s 2536e09.

The Telegram bridge (10-02) is "one more party on the store bus". It forwards Seer messages and waking junctures, advancing its cursors only after each send, and turns phone text into user rows that wake ctl wait. Commands that act directly were rejected: "Everything goes through the overseer." A phone message ended the deliberate PK experiment: "Decline. You can stop for now, that's exactly the data we were hoping for."

stack.py (10-04) supervises the proxy, viz, Laya and the bridge, backs off 2 to 60 s, and adopts services it didn't start. On 10-05 it restarted a crashed viz twice (junctures #276, #300).

9.8Laya: a local model for speech triage

Every line a player says near a harvest job holds the job until the Seer has read it (§6.8). The hold is safe but slow, and a gatherer who ignores a GM for about two minutes risks jail. So on 10-01 the owner asked whether a small local model could tell a staff member's attendance check from player chatter at once. Laya [15] is a ModernBERT-large encoder [26] (421M parameters) that answers typed yes/no questions over text in one forward pass, with no text generation. The harness asks it two questions about each line, with the nearby players and the recent speech in the prompt: check, is the speaker checking whether we are there, awake or human, asking what we are doing, or telling us to say or do something; and direct, is the line aimed at us. It runs in its own Python environment on the GPU beside the client, where a forward pass takes 59 ms against 901 ms on the CPU, in fp16 because Laya's default bf16 moved scores by up to 0.073, enough to cross the alarm threshold docs/NOTES.md "Laya speech triage".

Zero-shot, it could raise an alarm but not lift one. No staff speech had ever been captured, so the evaluation set (eval_triage.py) is 22 real player lines from the memory store and 25 GM-style lines we wrote. Across 16 question, checkpoint and prompt variants, no threshold could safely skip the hold: the one that kept holding every GM-style line would have skipped only 10 of the 22 player lines, and it sat exactly on the lowest GM-style score. The check question did separate the blunt checks. At 0.6 it caught 6 of 25 ("are you there?" 0.83, "This is a GM, please answer." 0.86) and alarmed on 1 of 22 player lines ("say 1"). The owner chose "shadow + escalate" from four options: every line still holds the job, and a check of 0.6 or more raises gm_suspected and the staff alarm the moment the line is scored. Each verdict is stored with how its hold ended, as labelled data for later docs/PLAN.md "Laya speech triage".

Synthetic data. On 10-04 the owner asked whether synthetic lines could fine-tune it. A search of the 97k captured Discord messages found players reporting that unanswered gatherers get jailed, but not one message quoting what staff actually say in a check. So every positive example would encode our own guesses: good enough to escalate sooner, never to skip a hold. harness/triage_data.py builds 1,057 prompts in exactly the format the live service sees, deterministically from a seed (Table 18):

  • GM checks aimed at us: 160 hand-written templates (presence pings, "are you a real person?", "type the word banana in chat please", "move one step to your left", jail warnings), each expanded four times with one of 24 names for us, one of five surface styles (as written, terse, lowercase, typo'd, chatspeak) and a scene: after silence, as a second ping, after our own line, or in the middle of other players' chatter. In 30% of them the speaker is hidden, not on screen. Our names never include the evaluation's Character Alpha, so a gain there cannot come from name matching.
  • Look-alikes that are not checks: the same wording aimed at another named player, friends pinging each other with context that shows who is meant, players talking to us without checking on us (including back-and-forths with our reply), trade and guild-recruitment ads (also as cycles of 2–5 ads from one player), pet commands, "say 1" headcounts, and chatter in Turkish, French, Portuguese, Czech and Japanese.
  • Real player lines from the memory store, plus Discord messages as a capped 25% of the player side for register and typos. Discord questions in the second person are skipped, since in a scene they could be aimed at us.

Near-duplicates within a class are dropped. The labels follow the two questions: a check aimed at us is check 1, direct 1; a player talking to us is 0, 1; everything else is 0, 0.

Evaluation first. Before any training, the stock checkpoint (pinned to one hub commit) was scored and the result frozen. Besides the 47 evaluation lines, 104 real player lines were held out: everything an evaluation speaker ever said, the one real conversation aimed at us, and 30% of the other texts by a stable hash. None of them enters training, not even as context, and any synthetic or Discord line too similar to one of them (difflib ratio 0.85) is dropped. The deployment rule was fixed in advance too: false alarms on the real held-out player lines must not increase, and catches on the GM-style lines must improve. Training used Laya's own fine-tuning recipe on the top 6 of 28 encoder layers plus the decision head (99.8M of 421M parameters): 4 epochs in 288 s on the laptop's GPU while the game client ran, under a 3.2 GB memory cap (Table 19).

Run 4 went live as v2 on 10-04. Gentle openers now alarm ("Hello?" 0.49 → 0.93, "you macroing?" 0.20 → 0.70), the six blunt checks stay caught, and "say 1" no longer alarms (0.69 → 0.53). Some things got worse: a Turkish dungeon-farm ad now crosses 0.6, indirect checks fell further ("anyone home" 0.45 → 0.13, "please respond" 0.32 → 0.22), and the shadow-only direct score now fires on lines aimed at nobody ("bank" 0.04 → 0.82). The weakness was written down at the time: every positive, in training and in the evaluation, was written by us, so the gain shows the model learned our idea of a check, not Outlands staff. The one test that rests on real data, held-out player lines not raising alarms, moved by a single line (5 → 4 of 104), on a set that had guided runs 2–4. Live, the stock model raised two staff alarms on 10-02, both at guild recruiters; none has fired since.

Lesson

Each model here earns its keep where something deterministic checks it: the Seer's moves by ctl's guards and the runners, the Discord extractor by substring grounding and author recounts, Laya by a hold that fires on every line anyway. Where nothing checked it, a hand-fought battle or a reply to a stranger the owner judged suspicious, the model was the weak link.

10Results

Ten days, 69 proxy sessions and 88 logged-in hours later, the harness was chopping about 1,300 logs per 22-minute trip with one character, and every CAPTCHA it saw was answered: 57 by its solver, 10 by the owner. This chapter collects the outcome numbers that cut across the other chapters: time, traffic, wood, skill, spot choice, hazards and money. All of them are taken at one snapshot, 2026-10-06 12:00 CDT. The final section says how far to trust them.

87.6 hlogged in over 69 proxy sessions (30.8 h with agent traffic)
94,295client packets injected by the agent: 18.8% of tagged C2S, 90% of all walk requests
32,676logs chopped in 4,125 successful chops; 23,003 boards stored by 86 trip rows
3,704logs/trip-h on the best completed trip (10-05), against 355 logs/trip-h for the three-trip Run 3 on 09-29; day aggregates 376 → 2,890 (10-05) and 3,341 (10-06 morning)
50.1 → 95.6Character Omega's Lumberjacking in about 38 hours
67/67harvest CAPTCHAs accepted (10 by the human, 57 by the solver)
31/34recall escapes that landed (median 2.13 s); two failures against one PK, one against a norse bear rider
12 + 1deaths, plus one deliberate demo death; 1 small theft (10 mandrake root)

10.1Where the hours went

Session length badly overstates how much the agent played. The proxy captured 87.6 hours of logged-in time. Counting only the wall-clock minutes that contain at least one client-to-server (C2S) packet tagged src=agent gives 30.8 agent-active hours. The same count over human-driven opcodes (walk, double-click, target, gump reply) gives 10.1 human-input hours, and the runners' own episodes add up to just 17.3 h (12.9 h of lumber trips, 4.4 h of hunt visits).

The shape of Figure 36 follows the project. 09-28 and most of 09-29 were human-only capture sessions, the owner playing while the proxy recorded. Agent traffic starts on 09-29 at session 20260929_142237. The busiest agent day is still 10-03 (8.37 agent-active hours; also the most logged-in hours, 22.6, most of them the idle Test Shard session), when Character Delta chopped the overworld and Character Kappa hunted; 10-05 comes close with 7.72. Character Omega's 9.65-hour daytime session on 10-05 carried 17,141 agent packets; the evening capture that followed it (16.3 h up to the snapshot, 12.0 h of them on 10-06) carried 21,186.

"Agent-active" measures the presence of injected traffic, not autonomy. Some of it was the Seer steering through ctl (§9).

On the wire, the agent sent 94,295 of the 517,644 C2S packets: 18.8% of the traffic that carries a source tag. The share depends heavily on the opcode. Measured against all C2S packets of each opcode (untagged ones included), the agent sent 90% of walk requests (0x02; 93% of the tagged ones), 99.2% of target replies (0x6C) and 86.7% of gump replies (0xB1; 89% of the tagged ones), but almost none of the background chatter (0.2% of 0xFF envelopes, no name queries), which kept coming from the stock client. §3 charts the per-day composition. One loose end: recounting the 2026-09-30 detection-surface audit's 11 sessions gives 67,991 C2S packets against the doc's 63,441. The agent count matches exactly (10,503), so the 4,550-packet gap lies in how the client's own packets were counted, by a basis we could not recover.

10.2Wood: logs chopped, boards stored

The runners chopped 32,676 logs in 4,125 successful chops; the 86 trip rows hold 28,448 logs and recorded 23,003 boards stored (412 on the Test Shard). The two numbers measure different things. "Chopped" comes from harvest_attempts, which records every chop; "stored" comes from trip rows. The gap is mostly about what got recorded, but not only. Until 2026-10-02 23:26 (5a33805) an aborted trip wrote no row at all, so on 10-01 Character Delta chopped 1,044 logs against one trip row, and on 10-02 3,374 against seven docs/NOTES.md l.369–373; memory DB. Conversely, "stored" in some rows includes carry-over from earlier trips (row 36: 334 logs, 796 boards stored; row 104: 1,030 logs, 2,410 boards, about 1,380 of them logs left unconverted by four aborted trips before it). About 1,500 logs were lost on the corpse in two deaths: trip 62 (1,070, Bastet) and trip 99 (≈428, an air dragon) docs/NOTES.md l.807, l.1112. And two stores were finished by hand and are missing from the rows: on 10-05 the overseer finished trip 92 after the convert loop gave up (the chest then showed 2,747 boards), and on 10-06 trip 120's 1,253 logs were converted and stockpiled with ctl act convert --store after a false thief alarm stopped the run at the landing memory DB chat 2026-10-06 11:40; docs/NOTES.md, "False thief alarm at the guild-house landing". Once the boards moved to the guild's Resource Stockpile on 10-05, it read 8,693 across five woods. The menu was not read again before the snapshot; since then the rows record 12,623 boards put into the stockpile, plus the 1,253 by hand, which would put it near 22,600 inferred.

More than half the wood came on one day. Figure 37 is flat until Character Delta started chopping on Shelter Island on 10-01, climbs once he left for the overworld on the afternoon of 10-02 and through 10-03, pauses for the home cutover on 10-04, and then turns almost vertical: 17,170 logs on 10-05 (53% of the total) across 41 trip rows, and 5,911 more in the morning of 10-06. Figure 38 shows the same arc trip by trip.

The last 23 rows (ids 100–122, all Character Omega) came from two overseer shifts after the earlier snapshot. The evening shift (Seer6, 20:15–23:25 on 10-05) wrote 14 rows with 8,008 logs and 8,033 boards stored, all into the stockpile; Lumberjacking went 81.1 → 90.5 docs/NOTES.md, Seer6 shift summary (ec339a1). After about 23:40 the client stayed logged in with no agent traffic until the morning shift (Seer7, from 09:50 on 10-06), which wrote 9 rows with 5,843 logs and 4,590 boards stored by the rows, plus trip 120's 1,253 by hand. Of the 23 trips, 15 ended early and 5 brought home nothing. Two ended in deaths: a norse bear rider at witcher_268 (10-05 20:43) and a snow elemental at the witcher_23 landing (10-06 10:14), after a world save delayed the recall arrival past the runner's 5 s wait. That second death cost the harvest-aspect armour set and the GM bronze hatchet docs/NOTES.md, "A late recall arrival left Omega at a hot landing"; ade127e. Since 10-05 21:24 a trip that escapes home by recall converts and stores before it stops (bddc446), so six of the new aborted trips stored boards.

Here a trip-hour is an hour of wall-clock trip time, from the start of a trip to its end, whether it stored or aborted. The baseline is Run 3 on 2026-09-29: 50 boards (= logs) in 8 min 25 s of trip time on Shelter Island, "about 355 boards per agent-active hour" docs/LUMBER_LOOP.md l.1436 at e1e024d, which is effectively 355 logs per trip-hour. Omega's best completed trips ran at 3,400–3,700 logs per trip-hour; trip 112 (10-05 22:49, witcher_23) brought in 1,747 logs in 28.3 minutes, 3,704 logs per trip-hour. One aborted trip ran faster: trip 103 chopped 868 logs in 13.0 minutes (4,000 logs per trip-hour) before a red player at 18 tiles sent it home, and its logs were stored on trip 104. The other half of the picture is the row of hollow markers along zero. From 10-03 (once aborted trips got rows), 45 of 68 trips ended early, 32 of them on a monster or player threat, and 22 of those 45 brought home nothing. Yet those aborts and empty trips are not why Omega's 10-05 day aggregate (2,890 logs per trip-hour) sits below his best trips: the 16 zero-log trips took only about 5% of the day's trip time, and without them the aggregate would be about 3,030. Most of the gap is the spread between spots and trips (trips 73 and 74 ran at about 1,500–1,600 logs per trip-hour, trip 111 at about 1,400, trip 77 at about 2,300). The morning of 10-06, with only greedy picks of known spots (§10.5), aggregated 3,341 logs per trip-hour over nine trips.

10.3Where the fourfold chop rate came from

The headline 10.4× (Omega's best completed trip, 3,704 logs per trip-hour, against Run 3's 355) compares one trip with a three-trip run. It splits into four factors: the chop rate rose ×4.66 (below), trip-time efficiency (the share of the chop-hour rate that survives into trip-hours) improved ×1.65, the best trip beat Omega's 10-05 day mean by ×1.28, and 09-29's day aggregate (376) sat ×1.06 above Run 3. Like for like, day aggregate against day aggregate, the rate rose 376 → 2,890 logs per trip-hour on 10-05 (×7.7) and to 3,341 in the morning of 10-06 (×8.9).

Logs per hour of chopping factor cleanly into three terms: how often a chop resolves, how often it succeeds, and how many logs a success yields.

Rchop=3600c×p×y‾
(19)

Here c is the median chop cycle in seconds, p = success / (success + fail) and y‾ is logs per success. On 09-29 those were 8.98 s, 0.31 and 7.93, which implies about 990 logs per chop-hour. On 10-05 they were 5.21 s, 0.82 and 8.11, which implies about 4,610; on the morning of 10-06, 5.33 s, 0.98 and 7.94, about 5,270. The measured trip-hour rate is lower on every day, because trips also spend time walking between stands, travelling, converting and storing.

The waterfall in Figure 39 divides the credit three ways.

  • Cycle time, ×1.72. The median cycle sat at 9–10 seconds for six days, then fell to 5.2 s when script-paced chopping went live on 2026-10-04 22:34. Its floor is the server's own 4.17 s chop plus about 0.75 s. §6 shows the gap distributions before and after, and the user's reasoning that every harvester on the shard already chops at script pace.
  • Success, ×2.64. This is the largest factor and the most confounded. The 09-29 number comes from Shelter Island, where harvest chance is roughly halved, at skill 60. The 10-05 number comes from the overworld at skill 52–90, and success kept rising with skill (0.98 on 10-06 at 90–96). Against the wiki formula, Omega's 14 trips with at least 20 attempts up to 10-05 20:30 produced 1,070 successes where 1,010.9 were expected (+5.8%). We suspect the Harvest Aspect armour's skill bonus, which the formula leaves out [inference].
  • Yield, ×1.02. A normal chop gives 5–10 logs. Chops of 12–20, all from 10-04 on, are the Aspect's "double yield" procs.
  • Not in the equation. Smart Harvest (target yourself; the server picks the tree) and home-based trips act on the gap between chop-hours and trip-hours. Home and travel overhead was only about 5% of trip time in Omega's 10-05 daytime trips; most of the roughly 37% gap on 10-05 is time inside the harvest phase that isn't chopping (walking to stands and trees, lockouts, CAPTCHAs, pauses).

10.4Skill

Only one of the three curves in Figure 40 shows earned progress. Character Omega went from 50.1 to 95.6 between 10-04 22:05 and 10-06 11:55: 456 updates over about 2,890 successful chops. The climb slows as the skill rises: about 3.8 successes per tenth of a point up to 81.2 (10-05 20:16), about 10.5 from 81.2 to 90.5, and about 14 from 90.5 to 95.6. Character Alpha's jump to 100 on 09-30 was typed into the Test Shard's player editor, so his 28 of 29 successful chops afterwards say nothing about training. Character Delta is the puzzle. He climbed from 60.1 to 69.1 on 10-01 and then gained nothing for two more days, through about 7,800 more logs. No document explains it. A total-skill cap or a skill lock are the obvious suspects [inference].

10.5Exploring spots

Choosing where to chop was left to the Thompson-sampling planner, which shipped on 2026-10-02 at 23:26 (§7). Its snapshot at 2026-10-06 12:00 shows how early in learning it still was. Of 132 candidate spots, 37 had a trip (38 counting Shelter Island, which the planner no longer lists). The 95 unvisited spots held about 87% of the probability of being best, the visited ones about 12%, because unvisited spots inherit an empirical-Bayes prior (3,166 logs per field hour) that sits above most measured posteriors (Figure 29). Figure 41 shows the behaviour that followed.

Before the planner, the first 18 trips went to four seeded venues (Shelter Island 10, Horseshoe Bay 5, Corpse Creek 2, Terran 1). Character Delta's 10-03 trips still mostly revisited known spots; the bend toward the diagonal came with Character Omega, who went to a new spot on 31 of his first 42 trips. That is the design working as intended ("Variation is required, not an inefficiency to remove", docs/LUMBER_LOOP.md l.411). The curve flattens at trip 112. During the evening shift the explore picks gave 262–392 boards each from small groves, and with the owner's goal set on boards the overseer switched to the planner's greedy pick (the best posterior net rate) from its 14th run on, passing it with --spot; the morning shift did the same docs/NOTES.md, Seer6 shift summary (ec339a1); 89130d8 added the greedy run to lumber plan. None of the 11 trips from 112 on went to a new spot, so these spot choices were not Thompson draws. Most spot estimates still rest on one trip: 25 of the 38 visited spots have exactly one, and per-trip logs are overdispersed by φ = 17.0 against a Poisson count.

10.6Hazards and escapes
