The harness lost a character to death twelve times, plus once on purpose. One small theft was seen (10 mandrake root). Table 21 collects the safety outcomes. The incident swimlane and the Bastet timing are in §8, the CAPTCHA solver and its latencies in §6.

Two lessons sit behind the table. The recall escape works against creatures and against PKs seen early, but not against a mage who recalls onto you: Bastet's spell landed 1.9 s after he appeared, faster than a 2.0 s cast. That pushed the defence into spot choice and exposure time. And early returns, more than deaths, are what cost wood. At 2.98 sent-home events per field-hour, the expected time before a trip is cut short is about 20 minutes of chopping, and every early return pays the travel overhead again.

10.7Money

Nothing was sold, so every wood figure in gold is a valuation. The 43 trip rows that carry a wood breakdown list 25,407 logs and boards (the newer rows break down the boards stored), 95.0% of them ordinary; at the board asking prices seen on 10-05 and 10-06 (ordinary 26.8 gp; goldenwood 70, verewood 170) they come to about 684k gp. Valuing the 5,860 trip-row logs without a breakdown as ordinary would add about 157k gp. These are asks, not sales docs/research/ECONOMY.md l.315; memory DB prices. Real gold moved in small amounts: 3,985 gp spent at vendors in 31 purchases (mostly a Mark scroll, a Recall scroll and a horse), and 2,785 gp earned by the secondary hunt loop over 36 New Player Dungeon visits and 173 kills, both unchanged since 10-04. Character Kappa's melee earned 16.92 gp/min, Character Delta's magery 6.06.

10.8How far to trust these numbers

  • Small samples. 86 trips; 25 of 38 spots have one trip; all three PK deaths came from one player; the theft model is pure prior.
  • Accounting. Logs chopped ≠ boards stored. Hours nest: logged-in 87.6 ≫ agent-active 30.8 ≫ runner episodes 17.3.
  • Confounded progress. Per-day rates mix characters, skill, venue, pacing, Smart Harvest, the Harvest Aspect (lost with the 10-06 10:14 death) and, from 10-05 22:49, greedy rather than sampled spot picks; the planner rescales only for skill. The 10.4× rise (best completed trip against a three-trip run; ×7.7 day aggregate against day aggregate) describes where we ended up. It is not an A/B test.
  • One snapshot. Every number here comes from a read-only copy of the memory DB taken at 2026-10-06 12:00 CDT and the proxy captures cut at the same time, while a runner was still working; rows written after 12:00 are left out.
  • Unresolved: the shard label and the audit's 4,550-packet discrepancy.

11Building it with AI agents

One person wrote 568 prompts over ten evenings and daytime check-ins; omp coding agents turned them into 389 commits. This chapter looks at how that worked: the scale of the conversation, which models did the work, how work was delegated, the rules the agents were held to, and where they went wrong.

568human prompts (76,100 characters, median 90)
19,319assistant turns, or 34 per prompt
23,399tool calls, or 41 per prompt
92subagents spawned by 64 task calls
389commits, about 1.5 prompts each
≈$1,640notional list-price model cost (plan quotas in practice)

11.1The shape of the work

omp (“Oh My Pi”) is the terminal coding-agent harness every session ran in. A top-level session is one chat; a subagent is a child session spawned with the task tool, which reports back with yield.

The build ran from the first prompt (“Hi”) on 2026-09-27 at 19:07 to the analysis snapshot on 2026-10-06 at 12:00 CDT. It produced 54 top-level sessions (43 on the laptop, 11 on the desktop) and 92 subagent sessions: 223.6 MB of JSONL logs. These totals, and every count in this chapter, leave out the two sessions that wrote and refreshed this paper. The laptop's logs are a copy taken on 2026-10-05 at 20:15 CDT, so any laptop activity after that is missing from these totals; the desktop logs run to the snapshot. The median session had 3 prompts and 22 had two or fewer, yet the five biggest session families account for 60% of all assistant turns. The first session, opened from an elevated shell in C:\Windows\system32, ran for 43 hours wall-clock and took 115 prompts omp session index, laptop.

Each human prompt bought 34 assistant turns and 41 tool calls. After a prompt, the median autonomous run lasted 1.9 minutes and 8 turns. The 90th percentile was 24.5 minutes, and 16 runs went past an hour. The longest real one was an overseer run on 10-02 that played for 170 minutes (118 turns) without a word from the owner; a later run that day reached 158 turns in 145 minutes. Prompts stayed short: half were under 90 characters, and only five were longer than 800. They were directions, not specifications.

The project had a clock. No prompt was typed between 00:00 and 08:59 on any day (Figure 43). The busiest prompting hour was 22:00, with 76 prompts. Agent work peaked a little earlier, at 17:00 (2,049 turns), and kept going into the 23:00 hour after the owner's last message. It almost never crossed midnight: only 23 turns happened after 00:00. Nothing ran unattended overnight. 23.9% of all prompts (136) were typed while an agent was still working, as mid-run steering.

11.2Models, limits and a relay baton

The project started on Kimi K3 on purpose: Anthropic's guardrails kept Claude Opus from doing the reverse engineering the project needed first, so for two days Kimi did everything, from the anti-cheat research to the cipher crack and the first proxy the owner, 2026-10-05. The provider was shaky, and so was the network. On 09-27 and 09-28 the logs show three socket closes and two 403 “You've reached your 5-hour usage limit” errors from the provider, plus four connection errors and one missing API key when the agent knocked the laptop offline while setting up a NIC alias (09-28 13:38–13:40) laptop session “Cracking UO XOR session cipher”. By 09-29 the owner judged the reverse engineering largely done, and Kimi had not managed to make injected walking work, so he switched models. At 13:54 he asked for “one brief handoff .md file for the next session to start from”. At 14:06 a new session opened with “Read @HANDOFF.md and continue work from where we last left off” and was switched to Claude Opus 5.5. The model changed hands at a document boundary, not in the middle of a conversation, and that set a pattern the project kept.

Opus did 87.9% of all assistant turns (16,975). Kimi did 10.7% (2,065) and came back only for small jobs and one notable evening (§11.6). Sonnet 5.5 did 1.4%, used on purpose for chores: babysitting the viz server, writing the Lord British persona, rebuilding the viz.

omp records a list-price cost for every turn. The owner was on subscription plans (the Kimi quota errors and the Anthropic OAuth credential records point that way), so read every dollar figure here as notional usage, not money spent.

At list prices the whole build comes to about $1,640: Opus $1,415, Kimi $213, Sonnet $12. Prompt caching is what made that affordable. 99.1% of Opus's input tokens were cache reads, 4.4 billion of them, against 35 thousand uncached input tokens. Cache reads still came to 62% of the Opus bill, because the average Opus turn carried about 260k tokens of context. Six times a session filled its window. Compaction kicked in at 750–850k tokens and summarised the context down to 22k–135k omp compaction records. Two of the six compactions hit the 10-04/10-05 desktop hub, which served as the project's control room for more than a day.

11.3Hub and spokes

Subagents arrived on 09-28 at 14:57, when the agent split off a metadata parser (MrtParser) on its own; the owner's first explicit request, “Launch an agent to work on the record-grammar hunt while we talk about Phase 2”, came at 17:16. They became routine on 09-29. In total, 64 task calls spawned 92 subagents (86 general workers, 3 reviewers, 2 scouts, 1 low-effort helper), and they produced 45% of all assistant turns. The hub writes a shared contract plus a # Target / # Change / # Acceptance brief for each child, and the children report back through yield and short IRC messages. One family ran at most 7 children at once. The whole corpus peaked at 10 sessions writing in the same ten-minute window. Subagents never spawned subagents.

The most interesting subagents were not builders at all. From 09-30 onward some children were told to play: “Act as the Seer: read docs/OVERSEER.md…”. They drove the character through harness/ctl.py while the hub kept engineering (the shifts themselves are in §9). Twenty such operator subagents logged 25.1 active hours and 2,211 turns for $72.8. That is about $2.9 per active hour, against about $14.1 per hour for the 67 builder and researcher subagents. Their tool mix shows why. Operators mostly ran bash (1,460 calls, the channel for every ctl status, act goto and know add) and blocked in wait. They made just 6 edit calls, while builders made 1,450. A good shift is cheap because the deterministic runner does the playing and the LLM mostly waits.

This split was not designed up front. The first Overseer subagents ran demos on the Test Shard on 09-30, but on 10-01 and 10-02 the owner had the main session itself “act as the Overseer”. On 10-02 it played for 8.4 active hours. That day produced 28 commits and only 27 subagent turns, the fewest of any day after the first. The fix came from the owner on 10-03:

You should probably start an overseer subagent and tell it what to do, since when you pause for long times leaving Character Delta in the wilderness he's liable to get killed

— the owner, omp session “Lumber spot optimizer near banks”, 2026-10-03 15:18

On 10-04 the desktop hub tried playing in the foreground once more. Six minutes in, the owner said: “Ok, stop acting as the overseer.” After that it sent out six Seer subagents in one day, with terse dispatch orders like “Send an overseer subagent back out, we need more boards!”.

For changes that could collide, the owner used git worktrees. There were five, for the guardrail scrub and CAPTCHA solver, the Ultima UI restyle, the Telegram bot, a test speedup and a paperdoll tweak. Each was merged back with a one-line prompt, once with the warning “I'm sure there will be conflicts because another agent was working on ctl” desktop session, 2026-10-04 17:37.

11.4Standing rules

Each session starts blank. What carries over is AGENTS.md, a 38-line file that every session reads first. Its rules came from specific moments (Table 22). Usually the owner said something once in chat and the agent wrote it into the file in the same turn.

One rule probably caused the problem it was later rewritten to prevent. The original AGENTS.md told agents to use Python 3.13 and spelled out its full path under C:\Users\first\AppData\… 56208c5. We suspect that line is why agents kept typing the full path. The owner complained about the wasted tokens twice, on 09-30 and 10-03, before the rule was rewritten to forbid it. The jq rule is the reverse case: an agent shell builtin that silently stood in for the real tool. The same commit history shows Rule 0 actually being followed. docs/NOTES.md is touched by 175 of the 389 commits (45%), and the four most-touched files in the repo are all documentation.

11.5How the owner steered

The owner's prompts came in three registers: goals at a high level (“Plan and implement whatever you can tonight using subagents. Please leave me a summary at the end of what is needed from me.”), game knowledge as short asides (“thieves look friendly to us until they steal”), and challenges to what the agent said about itself. The third mattered most.

The first challenge set the tone. On day 0 at 22:08 the owner asked whether the Outlands client encrypted its traffic. Kimi's answer, from string searches alone, was “Verdict: verified — no encryption on the wire”. The owner, steering mid-run: “Can you run a Wireshark analysis just to be sure?” The capture showed that client-to-server traffic was obfuscated. Within the hour the owner had walked his character west 20 times to produce known plaintext, and the XOR was cracked. Other challenges followed the same pattern: “Hold up. He only moved when I moved him with the arrow keys”, “I think you compared against an old screenshot”, and “I am not convinced there was an issue with the server detecting artificial movement”. Each one caught a wrong claim, though not always before it reached the docs. The evidence-first rule and the [INFERENCE] label give the agents a way to say what they have not checked. The owner's habit of asking for a measurement is what made those labels mean something.

Formal approval steps were rare: 14 ask calls and 4 plan-mode entries across 568 prompts. Steering was mostly by interruption, with 71 user aborts, 19 of them in the first session. The owner also acted as the agents' eyes and hands. He accepted UAC prompts they could not see, ran controlled experiments, solved CAPTCHAs, and popped a trapped pouch so an agent could capture the traffic.

11.6The guardrails episode

The clearest case of model behaviour changing the course of the work came on 09-30. That afternoon the owner decided to move the overseer off the Test Shard. At 17:04 he asked an Opus session to remove the Test-Shard-only restrictions from the docs. The day-0 AGENTS.md, drafted by an agent, said those constraints could only be lifted with “an explicit, informed acknowledgment of that risk in the conversation”. Opus's thinking cited exactly that, and it opened an ask titled “Getting informed acknowledgment of ban risk”. The owner cancelled the ask, and the session ended after four turns. A minute later he started a different Opus session that audited the harness's traffic for anything a stock client could not have produced.

That evening a broader version of the request went to Kimi K3: remove references to the shard's rules, reframe ANTICHEAT.md as evasion intelligence, and drop the requirement that a human solve CAPTCHAs. The 21:26 and 21:44 sessions each spent their thinking on whether this amounted to removing safety guardrails. The owner interrupted each one after a single turn. The third, started at 21:45 in a fresh worktree, did the job. It sent out seven doc-scrub subagents at 21:49, committed 2f60ad9 at 21:58, and was merged at 23:34. In all: 4 sessions, 2 models, 3 aborts, and about 23 minutes from the first Kimi attempt to the fan-out. The next morning the owner set CAPTCHAs back to human-solved by default, with an auto-solve toggle in the viz (d152c00).

Lesson

Rules written into the repo bind later sessions, and other models, more firmly than any chat message. A constraint an agent drafted on day 0 was still being enforced three days later, by a different session, after the owner had decided otherwise. If AGENTS.md is going to carry consent rules, the owner should write them as deliberately as code. The ethics of the shard move itself are discussed in §12.

11.7Two machines, one repo

On 10-04 the project moved from the laptop to the desktop. At 15:27 came “Make sure everything is stopped and then push the handoff so I can go resume on my desktop”. The desktop cloned the repo at 15:56. At 15:58 a single prompt, “Read @SETUP.md and setup this project for the first time on this Windows desktop”, started a 23-minute setup session. That session found hard-coded C:\Users\first paths in 55 files (54 changed in 06acc67), handing the 26 reverse-engineering scripts to a subagent and fixing the harness code itself. The runtime memory moved separately as a baton, through dbhandoff.py and the NAS (§5.8). Machine use was serial: only 3 ten-minute windows in the whole corpus show both machines active. The laptop wrote 300 commits and the desktop the last 89.

11.8What git shows

All 389 commits carry one author identity, although agent sessions wrote every one of them. The daily counts follow the session activity: 68 and 67 on 09-29/30, a lull of 17 on 10-01 (a ten-hour daytime gap), and the peak of 76 on 10-03 (Figure 45). Commits cluster at noon, 17:00 and late evening, with 31% of them (119 of 389) at 20:00 or later. Commit messages are long: the median full message is 148 characters, and 67 run past 500. In practice they work as a second lab notebook.

The codebase grew from 577 Python lines on the first night to 55,890 at the snapshot commit, about 97 times as many (Figure 46). The two biggest half-day jumps were 09-29 PM (the viz and the overseer groundwork, +13.4k) and 10-03 PM (Discord tooling, the dungeon crawl, Witcher runes, +9.3k). Test code stayed at roughly half the size of core code. By the end there were 231 def test_ functions and 1,789 assert/check sites, plus 131 viz test cases, and 49% of commits had touched a test file. That fits the owner's day-1 instruction: “the test suite is extremely important so make sure it is thorough and follow TDD”. Prose grew faster than code. The Markdown docs reached 197k words, not counting the generated Discord knowledge base, which is 3.5 words for every line of Python, and 28% of commits changed nothing but .md files. These counts leave out the paper itself (docs/paper/), committed on 10-05.

11.9How the agents failed, and what worked

The tool logs show the everyday friction (Figure 47). edit failed on 12.5% of calls. Most of those (398 of 523) were the anchored-edit protocol refusing an edit aimed at lines the agent had never been shown in its latest read. That cost retries, not corrupted files. bash failed 4.3% of the time, mostly on misused service flags, Python tracebacks, and the jaq null errors behind the jq.exe rule. wait took the most wall time, 41.5 hours, because that is where hubs blocked on children and Seers blocked on the game.

The costly failures were not tool errors. They were confident claims that turned out to be wrong (Table 23).

Four things did work. Documents as the baton: HANDOFF.md took the project across a model switch, and SETUP.md across machines, each in a single prompt. Delegation with a contract: named subagents with explicit acceptance criteria kept the hub free for conversation. Deterministic code with LLMs at the edges: it holds for the harness itself, and it is also why Seer shifts cost about a fifth as much per hour as builder sessions. A sceptical human: from the first night's “Did we verify whether it does or not?” onward, the owner kept asking for checks and kept watching the game screen.

Finding

In ten days and 76,100 typed characters, one person directing agents produced a 56k-line codebase, 197k words of design notes and a harness that played the game for hours at a time. Typing was clearly not the bottleneck; we think the owner's attention and game knowledge were. The agents' main weakness was overconfidence, and their most reliable defences were the owner's questions and the measurements those questions forced.

12Discussion

What we would tell someone starting this tomorrow, where the evidence is thin, and the parts that are not purely technical.

12.1Lessons

1. Put the LLM above the loop, not in it

Every attempt to let a language model act inside a reflex loop ended badly. The hand-fought dungeon hunt that killed Character Kappa in about fifteen seconds produced the rule we now quote most: "An LLM is way too slow to react for combat" (§8). The design that worked gives the model a database of junctures, a small CLI and a wake-up call, and leaves chopping, walking and fleeing to code with typed failures (§9). The model's best contributions were judgement calls no controller could make: abandoning an unworkable grove, noticing a pattern across shifts, writing up what went wrong.

2. A shared store is the cheapest integration layer

Putting every event, trip, chat line and fact into one SQLite file gave us a message bus, an analytics warehouse, a training set for the planner and the paper's own results chapter for the price of one schema (§5). The costs were real: a store of 352 MB by the snapshot (179 MB when it was handed between computers like a baton), a visualizer whose slow LAN reader fell further and further behind (147 s after 200 s in a replay with a reader throttled to 1.5 MB/s) until its state updates were trimmed, and constant care about who is allowed to write.

3. Model uncertainty, then act on samples of it

The planner never needed to be right about any one spot. Thompson sampling plus honest posteriors (and a prior that says how many logs a grove can hold) produced "almost always exploring" behaviour at the start, which the owner insisted was exactly right for a Bayesian process with 132 candidate spots, of which only 37 had a trip by the snapshot (§7). Late on 10-05, after explore picks had brought home 262–392 boards a trip, the Seer proposed taking the planner's greedy pick instead, the main session agreed ("the goal is boards"), and the overnight shifts exploited (§9). The same discipline caught real mistakes: aborted trips that had been silently flattering dangerous spots, and a board price assumed at 9.5 gp that the market put at 26.8.

4. The field report loop is the product

The most valuable feedback came from the Seer playing live and posting what hurt: a runner idling next to an air dragon, a door that ate a step, a landing rune eight tiles off. A coding agent in the main session fixed it, a test pinned it, the next shift ran on the fix. Over the last three days that loop closed in well under an hour per issue. We think this, more than any single algorithm, is why a ten-day project reached 3,700 logs per trip-hour on its best completed trip (§10).

5. Write it down, or it did not happen

Rule 0 (record and push engineering knowledge before a session ends) turned out to be the project's real memory. Sessions ended, models changed, two computers took turns, and nothing was lost because every finding was in docs/NOTES.md or docs/PLAN.md. Its price is a 226 KB notes file that touched 45% of all commits; its payoff is that a fresh agent on a fresh machine rebuilt the working stack in about half an hour (§11).

12.2Working with the agents

The owner set the goals and made the product and risk calls; the agents worked out most implementation designs within them inferred. We have no tally of decisions by origin; the record at ee59524 holds 32 owner-decision markers in docs/NOTES.md and 19 in commit messages (counting "user decision" and "(user, …)"-style attributions), against a far larger body of unattributed design. Prompts were short (median 90 characters), and the owner's most useful moves were interrupting, asking "can you measure that?", and supplying game knowledge the agents could not look up ("thieves look friendly to us until they steal"). Two of the biggest wins started as the owner's hunches: moving the overseer from a bespoke daemon to an omp session talking to a CLI, and making subagent play the standing practice (10-03) so the main session could keep engineering (an agent had first used an overseer subagent on 09-30).

The agents' characteristic failure was confident wrongness that propagated into the docs: a day of conclusions built on a mis-decoded stream, a "gate" that was actually the client's own state, a claim of "movement solved" that a quick look at the screen contradicted. The cure was cultural, not technical: evidence-first prose, [INFERENCE] labels, and an owner who kept asking for a capture. We also recorded a milder pattern: one agent asked for informed acknowledgment of the ban risk; two others hesitated in their thinking and were interrupted; the owner then re-sent the same instruction, unchanged, to a fresh session in a new worktree, which complied (§11.6).

12.3Limitations

  • One game, one skill, one week. Everything measured is lumberjacking plus a little hunting. The planner's structure should transfer to mining or fishing; we have not tried.
  • Small samples. Eighty-six trips over three characters, 25 of the 37 planner spots with a trip having just one (38 counting Shelter Island, which the planner excludes), three PK deaths, all to one player (Bastet), plus eleven other hostile players escaped by a clean recall. Rates like the 0.040 creature deaths per field hour will move: that is the planner's posterior (prior 0.01/h over 20 pseudo-hours) and counts only one of Omega's five creature deaths; raw, it is 1 attributed creature death in 9.8 field hours.
  • Confounded progress. Throughput rose from about 355 logs per trip-hour (a three-trip Shelter Island run on 09-29) to 3,704 on the best completed trip, late on 10-05 (2,890 for 10-05 as a whole, 3,341 for the morning of 10-06), but the rise mixes a faster chop cycle, a better success rate, a different character, a different venue, Harvest Aspect armor and, from the evening of 10-05, greedy spot picks. §10 decomposes what it can; it is not a controlled experiment.
  • Notional costs. The $1,640 of model spend in §11 is list price for an owner on subscription plans.
  • A moving target. Outlands patches its client and rules. During the project, what changed was mostly our understanding of its mechanics: the stationary-harvest penalty (a 2025 rule) was decoded on 10-03, and Smart Harvest, a long-standing feature, was adopted on 10-04. Every rate here is "that week".

12.4Ethics and the shard's rules

This project automates play on a shard whose published rules prohibit unsanctioned automation. We did it knowingly, as a personal engineering project on the owner's own accounts, and we said so in the repo. The early constraints (Test Shard only, a human solves every CAPTCHA) were relaxed by the owner on 09-30, and the agents' hesitation about that is part of the record (§11.6). Several things stayed fixed throughout: the harness never attacks other players, never speaks about itself in game, never touches the client or its files, and treats a staff member in view as a reason to stop. Whether any of that makes it acceptable to the shard's community is a separate question, and the answer from the shard's own rules is no. The owner bears that risk, which is one reason this document is a private record and not a recipe.

There is also a small ecosystem point. A harvest bot competes for the same groves as human lumberjacks, and the planner's explicit objective is to out-earn them. The harness's rule that it never fights players protects the other characters; it does not make the competition fair.

12.5Conclusion

In ten days a person and a handful of AI coding agents built a system that played a twenty-nine-year-old MMO for 31 hours of agent-driven time, chopped 32,676 logs, answered every CAPTCHA, and improved its own choices from its own records. The parts that carried the weight were unglamorous: a proxy that forwards almost everything unchanged, a world model that forgets what the client forgets, a database every component can write to, a planner that admits it does not know yet, and an LLM that is allowed to be slow because nothing urgent depends on it. The agents wrote most of the code and, we believe, worked out most of the implementation designs; the owner decided what mattered and what not to do. The next thing to learn is how much of that division of labour survives when the problems are harder than chopping wood.

AProject timeline

The ten days from the first research prompt on 2026-09-27 to the 389th commit on 2026-10-06, the last before the 12:00 CDT snapshot, one entry per milestone, wrong turn or decision, grouped by day.

Times are local (CDT, UTC−5), the zone of every commit. Most entries carry the commit that landed the change as a source pointer. Entries without one come from the omp session logs (a user message, a live event the agent reported) or from the memory store. Filled dots mark the milestones the rest of the paper keeps returning to. The list merges three research datasets: the git-derived milestone list, the early-session timeline (09-27 → 10-01), and the late-session timeline (10-02 → 10-05), plus the commits, docs/NOTES.md and store junctures from 10-05 20:30 to the snapshot. Where they disagree on a time, we used the commit time. Live in-game events use the time the session log or the store recorded them.

A few patterns are easier to see here than in the chapters. Each day has one dominant theme: the cipher on 09-27/28, movement and the decode correction on 09-29, the overseer and the audit on 09-30, safety on 10-02/03, home logistics on 10-04/05, and on the morning of 10-06 fixes for what the lumber shifts ran into. No commit landed between 01:00 and 08:59, and 31% (119 of 389) landed at 20:00 or later git log ee59524. Wrong turns are usually corrected within the same day. The longest-lived mistake, the S2C "phantom dialect", lasted about 24 hours (§3).

BRepository map and code metrics

Every module in the repository at the snapshot commit, grouped by layer, with its line count and a one-line purpose, followed by the tests, the reverse-engineering scripts and the documents.

The numbers are physical lines (newline counts) in the committed blobs at ee59524 (2026-10-06 11:49 CDT, commit 389, the last before the 12:00 snapshot); commit counts per file leave out the 4 merge commits (389 = 385 + 4). The paper itself (docs/paper/, committed on 2026-10-05) is left out of every count here data/21_loc_by_layer.json. All 389 commits carry one author identity. In practice omp coding-agent sessions wrote them at the owner's direction: 300 on the laptop, then 89 on the desktop after it was cloned on 2026-10-04 at 15:58.

harness/            84 modules, 35,756 lines (the system itself)
  uo/  world/       wire codecs; packet-driven world model
  data/  testdata/  committed fixtures: rune libraries, captcha font, gump captures
  test_*.py         41 unit/integration suites, 13,436 lines
test_*.py           5 end-to-end suites at the root, 5,508 lines

ghidra_scripts/     23 Java scripts, 1,397 lines
*.py *.ps1 *.bat *.cmd  24 RE and operations scripts at the root, 1,492 lines
docs/  docs/research/  docs/missions/   29 Markdown files (root + docs/)
logs/               10 committed capture sessions

Two things stand out. The code is top-heavy at both ends. The lumber runner (loop_lumber.py, 3,550 lines) and the overseer's CLI (ctl.py, 3,412) are the two largest files and also the two most-changed code files (80 and 75 commits). The wire layer, which took the first two days, is comparatively small: the proxy itself is 1,087 lines, and the codecs under uo/ are about 670. The project also writes more prose than code: the prose docs (196,525 words, excluding the generated Discord digest) outnumber Python lines 3.5 to 1, and docs/NOTES.md alone was touched by 175 of the 385 non-merge commits data/21_loc_by_layer.json; data/11_loc_growth.json; git log --no-merges ee59524. Rule 0 of AGENTS.md asks every session to leave its knowledge in the repository, and these numbers are what that rule looks like over ten days.

B.1Harness modules by layer

Purposes are condensed from each module's docstring. Each table is sorted by size. Several modules could sit in two layers. For example, agent_gate.py lives in the runners table but is enforced inside the proxy; memory.py is written by the proxy and read by everyone (§5). We placed each one where its main caller lives.

Most suites run offline against captured sessions or stand-ins (a fake Bot API, a simulated game server speaking the real wire format), and none of them connects to the game server. The pattern that dominates the later days is visible in the end-to-end runner tests: every live incident becomes a scenario that fails against the old code. C.3Client → server packets the harness sends

Every agent packet is built by harness/actions.py in the byte layout the stock client uses for the same gesture, padded to the client's length table. The counts are agent-originated packets across all 69 desktop session logs up to 2026-10-06 12:00 CDT. For scale, the human's client sent 306,060 0xFF packets over the same logs, most of them keepalives.

Builders also exist for vendor sell (9F) and prompt and text-entry replies (9A, AC, C2). The login (91), character select (5D) and the keepalive are always the client's own.

C.4Server → client packets the harness reads

The world model has handlers for 46 S2C ids and 17 C2S ids. Every parsed id parses on every real packet in the 18 reference captures. The table groups the ones that matter by what the harness does with them.

The proxy also writes three kinds of packet to the client alone, encoded with the session key, which never reach the server. A 0x21 re-anchors the client's display after an agent step. A 0x6C cancel takes down a cursor the agent already answered. A 0xBF sub 4 closes a gump the agent already answered. Over the 69 desktop logs up to 2026-10-06 12:00 CDT that came to 55,016, 8,267 and 2,251 packets respectively (method of brief 02 §3.3). Why these exist is told in §3.

C.5File formats

DThe planner's Bayesian model, step by step

This appendix spells out the statistics behind §7: what each symbol means, why each distribution was chosen, how evidence updates it, and how the planner turns posteriors into one runner command. It ends with one spot worked through by hand at the snapshot. Everything here describes harness/lumber_opt.py at ee59524; the numbers come from the same read-only planner run as Figure 29.

D.1Notation

Gamma distributions are written with shape and rate, Gamma(α,β), so the mean is α/β and the variance α/β2. Every rate is per field hour: time in the grove from the first tree to leaving, walking between trees included, travel lockout excluded. Weighted sums run over a spot's trips with the recency weights wi, and a subscript w marks a weighted count (for example diedw is the sum of the weights of the spot's deaths).

D.2Counts, rates and conjugate updates

Logs arrive while the character stands in a grove, so the natural model for a trip's haul is a count in an exposure time: L|λ∼Poisson(λH). The Gamma distribution is the conjugate prior for a Poisson rate [11]: if λ∼Gamma(α0,β0) before a trip, it is Gamma again after it, and updating is addition.

λ∼Gamma(α0,β0),L|λ∼Poisson(λH)⟹λ|L∼Gamma(α0+L, β0+H)
(20)

That makes α0 a pseudo-count of logs and β0 a pseudo-exposure in hours. The posterior mean is a weighted average of the prior mean and the spot's own rate, with weights in proportion to exposure. This is the "shrinkage" that keeps a single lucky trip from crowning a spot:

𝔼[λ|L]=α0+Lβ0+H=β0β0+Hμ+Hβ0+H⋅LH
(21)

The same pattern repeats for every quantity the planner learns. Rates of events (sightings, deaths, early returns, thefts) are Gamma posteriors over field hours. Proportions (P(death | sighting), the yielding share of trees, the share a thief takes) are Beta posteriors, the conjugate prior of a binomial proportion, where Beta(a,b) reads as a pseudo-successes and b pseudo-failures. Conjugacy keeps the model to arithmetic with no sampler to tune, and every posterior can be drawn from in one call.

D.3Overdispersion: why a trip counts less than its logs

Logs are not single events. A successful chop yields a lump of about eight (32,676 logs from 4,125 successes at the snapshot), so a trip's haul is a compound Poisson count: N successes at rate ν, each yielding Yj logs. Its variance is larger than its mean by a fixed factor:

𝔼[L]=νH𝔼[Y],Var⁡[L]=νH𝔼[Y2]⟹Var⁡[L]𝔼[L]=𝔼[Y]+Var⁡[Y]𝔼[Y] ≥ 𝔼[Y]≈8
(22)

A plain Poisson update would treat 4,000 logs as 4,000 independent events and become far too sure of itself. The planner uses the quasi-Poisson fix from generalized linear models [17]: assume Var⁡[L]=ϕ𝔼[L], estimate ϕ from the trips, and divide both the count and the exposure by it. L/ϕ then has mean and variance both equal to λH/ϕ, like a Poisson count in exposure H/ϕ, and the conjugate update applies to it unchanged; that is Eq. (10). The estimate is Pearson's statistic over trips of at least three minutes, each against its own spot's rate:

ϕˆ=max⁡(8, 1n−k∑s∑i∈s(Li−λˆsHi)2λˆsHi),λˆs=∑i∈sLi∑i∈sHi
(23)

with n trips over k spots that have at least two of them. The floor of 8 is the compound-Poisson minimum above. The measured 17.0 says trips at one spot also differ for other reasons (other lumberjacks, interruptions, different stands). In practice an hour of chopping at about 4,000 logs counts as about 235 independent events, so the rate's coefficient of variation after one field hour is about 1/235≈6.5%.

D.4Recency weights

Each trip's likelihood is raised to the power wi=0.5agei/14d (Eq. (7)). In a conjugate model that simply multiplies the trip's counts and exposure by wi, which is why every sum in the planner is weighted. This is the idea of a power prior [5]: old data is not deleted, it is discounted, so a two-week-old trip counts half and a four-week-old one a quarter. The prior itself is not discounted, so a spot nobody has visited for months drifts back towards "a spot like the others". The half-life is a design choice, not an estimate: it encodes the belief that competition, killers and patches change on that time scale.

D.5The empirical-Bayes prior

The prior for an unvisited spot is learned from the visited ones [4]. Take the weighted rate λˆs of each of the m spots with at least half a weighted field hour, use their mean μ and sample variance, floor the spread at 35% of the mean, and choose the Gamma with that mean and variance (moment matching):

s02=max⁡(1m−1∑s(λˆs−μ)2, (0.35μ)2),α0=μ2s02,β0=μs02
(24)

At the snapshot the floor binds: μ=3,166 logs per field hour, α0=1/0.352=8.16, β0=0.00258. Because the prior enters the ϕ-scaled update, its weight in real field time is ϕβ0=0.044 h: after about 2.6 minutes of chopping, a spot's own data carries as much weight as the prior, and a typical first trip outweighs it several times over. Until then the spot is drawn from the full spread of the measured spots, which is what makes unvisited spots attractive to the sampler. "Empirical" means the prior is estimated from the same store it is applied to, so the uncertainty in μ itself is ignored. Only m=7 spots had the half weighted field hour needed to shape μ at the snapshot, so that is a real approximation.

D.6Hazards: competing clocks with partial pooling

Deaths, early returns and thefts are modelled as independent Poisson processes that run only during field time. Each has a per-spot Gamma posterior whose prior is centred on a rate pooled over every trip:

h‾=h0n0+∑all iwiein0+∑all iwiFi,hs∼Gamma(Sh‾+∑i∈swiei,  S+Es)
(25)

Here ei counts the trip's events, h0 and n0 are the global prior rate and its weight in pseudo-hours, and S is how many field hours of evidence the pooled rate counts for at one spot. Rare events lean hard on the pool: thefts use S=20 h and deaths 10 h, while early returns, which are common, use only 2 h. This is partial pooling, the middle ground between one rate for all spots and an independent rate per spot. Strictly, it is a two-stage empirical-Bayes shortcut: the pooled means are plugged in as known, not given their own posterior.

The death rate gets a structured prior. If hostile players appear at rate σs and each appearance kills independently with probability π, fatal encounters form a Poisson process of rate σsπ (thinning); creature deaths arrive independently at hC and simply add (superposition):

m0=σsπ[pvp]+hC,π∼Beta(1+pkw, 3+seenw−pkw)
(26)

The Beta(1, 3) prior on π says "one death in four sightings" with the weight of four sightings. By the snapshot the weighted evidence (about 30 weighted sightings, 3.5 weighted PK deaths) had moved it to Beta(4.53, 29.78), mean 0.132. Because sightings are far more common than deaths, a spot with many sightings but no deaths yet still looks dangerous. The cost is that each PK death counts twice, once in π and once in its own spot's count, which §7.4 flags.

D.7Thompson sampling and P(best)

The planner never maximizes a posterior mean directly when it explores. It samples a whole world from the posterior, finds the best spot in that world, and repeats [24] [22]. One draw for one eligible spot is:

  1. λ∼Gamma(αs,βs) and T∼𝒩(T‾s, sds), floored at 10 s;
  2. σ∼Gamma(⋅) (PvP spots only) and π∼Beta(⋅), then hD∼Gamma(10m0(σ,π)+diedw, 10+Es): a hierarchical draw, the prior's parameters first, the rate second;
  3. hS and hT from their Gamma posteriors, and ψ∼Beta(⋅), which fixes the grove's capacity;
  4. the value of the draw: maxQ⁡Rate(Q) under those parameters, over every other point of the trip-size grid, with Q capped by the capacity.

The creature rate hC and the theft share f are not drawn; they enter at their pooled means. Note what is random: the draw samples parameters (what we do not know), while the renewal-reward formula below averages over the outcomes of a trip (what chance will do) in closed form. Each draw is therefore an expected rate in one plausible world.

Pr⁡(best=s)=Prθ∼p(θ|𝒟)⁡[s=arg⁡maxs′⁡ maxQ⁡ Rates′(Q;θs′)] ≈ 12000∑r=12000𝟙[s wins draw r]
(27)

The Monte Carlo standard error is p(1−p)/2000, about 0.004 at the largest P(best) of 0.030. The pick itself is the winner of one more, fresh draw, so each spot is chosen with probability equal to its P(best): Thompson sampling is probability matching. The greedy spot is the one with the highest value at the posterior means, computed with the refined trip size. The pick is labelled explore when it differs from the greedy spot.

Figure 49 shows why P(best) was close to uniform at the snapshot. witcher_23 is well measured, and its draws stay between 2,585 and 3,273 logs/trip-h (10th to 90th percentile). Each of the 94 eligible spots nobody had visited draws from the wide prior, so in every round some of them land far above that, and the best of 123 draws has a median of 4,710. The sampler is not claiming that unvisited spots are better on average (witcher_279's median draw is 2,479); it is saying that one of them might be, and that the only way to find out is to go. That is also why the greedy pick and P(best) can disagree so sharply, and why the overseer could choose the greedy pick once the owner's goal was boards rather than information (§9).

D.8Renewal-reward with competing hazards

A trip is one cycle of a renewal process: overhead, field time until the quota or a hazard ends it, and a recovery delay after a death. By the renewal-reward theorem [21] the long-run rate is the expected reward of a cycle over its expected length, a ratio of expectations rather than the expectation of a ratio, so it is enough to compute two expectations per trip size:

Rate(Q)=B(Q)−supplies−GPD𝔼[cycle time],𝔼[cycle time]=T+E1(h,tf)+RPD
(28)

The trip ends at the first of three times: the quota time tf=Q/λ, a death clock τD∼Exp(hD), or a sent-home clock τS∼Exp(hS). The first of two independent exponential clocks is exponential with rate h=hD+hS, and it is a death with probability hD/h. So the trip survives to t with probability e−ht, and:

E1(h,x)=∫0xe−htdt=1−e−hxh,𝔼[field time]=E1(h,tf),PD=hDE1(h,tf),PS=hSE1(h,tf)
(29)

Since PD+PS+e−htf=1, no trip size can produce a death probability above 1, which is the bug the first, square-root sizing rule had on long trips. Thefts do not end the trip; each removes the share f of what is carried. Because they arrive at rate hT independently of the load, the expected load obeys a linear equation:

dCdt=λ−hTfC=λ−kC⟹C(t)=λ(1−e−kt)k
(30)

The logs stored are the load at the quota time if the trip survives that long, or the load at the moment it is sent home. A death stores nothing:

B(Q)=e−htfC(tf)+hS∫0tfe−htC(t)dt=e−htfC(tf)+hSλk[E1(h,tf)−E1(h+k,tf)]
(31)

As k→0 (no thefts) C(t)=λt and the integral becomes λE2(h,tf) with E2(h,x)=∫0xte−htdt=(1−e−hx−hxe−hx)/h2; the code switches to that form, and to series expansions for tiny hx, to avoid cancellation (_e1, _e2). With every term in closed form, the planner evaluates Rate on a 41-point log-spaced grid of trip sizes from 200 to 10,000 logs, then refines the best one by golden-section search to 10 logs. The rate is flat near its maximum, which is why the Thompson draws can use every other grid point.

D.9One spot by hand: witcher_23

witcher_23 was the greedy best at the snapshot. Table 39 walks its numbers from trip rows to the planner's value, using the equations above.

Two things stand out. The spot's own evidence dominates the rate (96% of the weight) after only 1.1 weighted field hours, but its capacity estimate is almost pure prior, so the number that binds the trip is the least informed one. And 40% of trips there are expected to be sent home before the quota, which is why the expected haul (571) is well below the quota (756).

D.10What is not fully Bayesian

  • Plug-in hyperparameters. The pooled hazard rates, μ, s0 and ϕ are point estimates; only π among the pooled quantities is drawn. A full hierarchical model would widen every spot's draws a little.
  • Fixed means inside the draws. hC and f enter every draw at their pooled means, and the regrowth window is an isotonic point fit (Figure 28), not a posterior.
  • Independence. A spot's rate, overhead and hazards are drawn independently, though a crowded grove is plausibly both slower and more dangerous. Hazards accrue only in field time, so a death at a landing is counted against the spot but adds no exposure.
  • Deterministic corrections. The skill rescaling (Eq. (9)) trusts the wiki's success formula exactly, and the overhead posterior is a weighted Normal with a 30 s floor on the spread rather than a conjugate Normal model.
  • Double use of PK deaths in π and in the spot's count, as noted above.

We have not measured how much each simplification matters. The uncertainty that shapes the plan at the snapshot is a different one: 94 of the 123 eligible spots had never been tried (Figure 49).

EGlossary

Ultima Online, Outlands and project jargon used in this paper, alphabetically. Packet ids are in Appendix C.

Agent gate
The harness's pause button, kill switch, forced-break timer (about every 2 h, jittered) and 8 h/day budget. The proxy checks it before every injected packet; the human's own traffic is never gated.
Aspect
Outlands' gear-specialisation system. A full set of Harvest-aspect armor (hue 2086) adds effective skill and a chance of double yield, so the lumber runner checks it before every trip.
Bastet
A mounted player killer whose title line read "Serial Killer [Prevalia]". Bastet killed our lumberjacks three times on 10-02 and 10-03, which is where recall-on-sight came from (§8).
Board / log
Trees yield logs; logs are converted into boards, the stored product. On 2026-10-05 a regular board was worth about 26.8 gp.
Captcha
Outlands' anti-automation dialog for harvesters: a gump with a number to type, about every 5–10 minutes. Three wrong answers block harvesting for 6 h.
Characters
Character Alpha (Test Shard, from 09-28), Character Delta (fresh Young character from 10-01), Character Kappa (an Arcane Mage, 10-03), Character Omega (the Guild, from 10-04), and Character Zeta (holds the rental room; 0.37 h on 10-05, never agent-driven).
ClassicUO
The open-source UO client. Outlands ships its own fork of it, compiled with NativeAOT and with Razor built in.
Cliloc
The client's numbered table of localised strings (Cliloc.enu). Many server messages arrive as a cliloc number with arguments, e.g. 502406, "This book needs time to recharge."
ctl
harness/ctl.py, the command-line API through which the Seer (or a human) reads state, runs tasks, acts in game and answers junctures. Every call prints exactly one JSON object.
The Guild
Character Omega's guild. Its guild house holds a rune library of 36 tomes and 839 runes, and a house steward that leads to Character Zeta's rental room, Omega's home.
Fastwalk key
A 32-bit token carried in each walk packet. The server hands tokens out (login usually ends on 8 and most re-arms carry 1, but the server also sends other small values; the proxy copies whatever it was given) and Outlands, unlike stock server emulators, checks them.
Gump
A server-defined dialog window: a layout of text, images, buttons and text entries. Runebooks, room menus, shelves and the captcha are all gumps.
Heat of Battle
The state after fighting a player, during which recall is blocked. It is one reason the harness never attacks players.
Juncture
An event on the overseer bus (table junctures) that can wake the Seer: a threat, a failed or finished task, nearby speech, a captcha, a death, possible staff. The store held 377 juncture rows at the 2026-10-06 12:00 CDT snapshot.
Landing
The tile a recall arrives on. The planner picks the rune whose landing is nearest the chosen grove and remembers landings that went wrong.
Laya
An encoder model (ModernBERT-large, 421M parameters) that answers yes/no questions about a line of text in one forward pass. Here it triages speech heard near a harvest job ("is this an attendance check?"), served locally on the GPU and fine-tuned once.
Memory store
harness/data/harness.db, the SQLite file in which the harness keeps everything it experiences and learns: the event log, walk and harvest memory, trip rows, the overseer bus and the Seer's knowledge table. Runtime data, never committed (§5).
Moongate
A public teleporter with a destination menu. On Shelter Island, taking one asks the player to renounce Young status.
Multi
A many-piece structure, usually a house, that the server sends as one item whose graphic is an index into multi.mul. The harness expands multis into walls and doors so that routes stop running into houses.
NativeAOT
.NET's ahead-of-time compilation to native machine code. The Outlands client is not a managed assembly, so there is no plugin loading and no IL decompiler shortcut; reverse engineering went through Ghidra and the binary's reflection metadata.
Notoriety (noto)
A per-mobile reputation code in the mobile-update packet: 1 blue (innocent), 2 green (ally; the harness treats it as blue), 3–4 grey (attackable, criminal), 5 orange, 6 red (murderer), 7 invulnerable (NPCs, vendors, staff).
NPD
The New Player Dungeon on Shelter Island, where Character Alpha's death demo took place and where the hunt runner first fought.
omp
The AI coding-agent harness that wrote this project. The Seer also runs on it, as an omp session or subagent.
Razor
The UO assistant (macros, hotkeys, scripts) built into the Outlands client and the only sanctioned automation. Razor scripts can't walk on Outlands (removed 2023-07), and Outlands can gate them from the server.
Recall
A Magery teleport to the location marked on a rune, cast as a spell or spent from a book's charges. It takes about 2 s and can be disturbed by damage. It is the harness's escape and its way to and from work.
Red / PK
A player killer. "Red" refers to notoriety 6, the murderer's name colour. Our threat model doesn't treat colour as proof either way: a thief looks blue until the moment of the steal.
Rental room
Outlands' inn-room housing. Nobody can follow you in and no recall reaches inside, so since 10-04 lumber trips end there.
Rune, runebook, rune tome
A rune marks one location to recall to. A runebook holds runes, recall charges and a default rune. A rune tome is a larger Outlands book (up to 26 rows) that opens only within 2 tiles.
Rune library
A collection of locked-down tomes others can use: the public Cambria library (14 tomes, 360 runes, including the 359 numbered Witcher runes) and the Guild house (36 tomes, 839 runes).
Secure chest
A locked-down container in the rental room that only its owners can open. Boards went there until the stockpile took over.
Seer, the
The LLM overseer: an omp agent session that supervises the deterministic runners through ctl, wakes on junctures, and talks to the owner in the viz and on Telegram. It was named on 2026-10-03 and given Hawkwind's voice (§9).
Shelter Island
Outlands' new-player island. Harvesting there needs Young status, halves the harvest chance and caps skills at 80, but no hostile player actions are possible.
Smart Harvest
Answering the hatchet's target cursor with yourself instead of a tree: the server then chops whatever harvestable tree is nearby. Adopted 2026-10-04.
Stationary Penalty
An Outlands rule: after a recall or teleport, or after about 5 minutes standing still, harvesting fails until you walk 5 steps.
Steward
The house NPC whose context menu ("Room" → "Visit Other Rooms") leads into a house's rental rooms. Leaving the room by its door returns you to the steward.
Stockpile
A Resource Stockpile: Outlands storage for raw materials, added to the room on 2026-10-05. It holds boards by kind and read 8,693 boards after the chest was emptied into it.
Storage shelf
A container that keeps a per-character loadout: "Resupply" tops the backpack up to it, "Restock" puts surplus and spent items back.
Test Shard
Outlands' public test server. Houses and inn rooms are wiped every day at midnight UTC. The project started there with Character Alpha.
Trapped pouch
A pouch that explodes when opened. The runner stashes logs in one so that a thief who snoops it sets off an alarm: "a delay plus an alarm, not a lock".
Walk sequence
The 8-bit counter in every walk packet: starts at 0, wraps from 255 to 1, and the server accepts only the value it expects next. The proxy keeps one shared ladder for the human's and the agent's walks.
WinDivert
A Windows packet-diversion driver. The harness uses it as a small user-space NAT that redirects the client's port-2593 connection to the local proxy, because the client ignores its own server settings.
Witcher runes
A community rune set laid out by a player called Witcher for treasure hunting: about 359 numbered runes spread across the wilderness, publicly available in Cambria. They became the lumber planner's gateway to the whole map.
Young
New-player status. It protects starting items and gives access to Shelter's bank, vendors and harvesting. It is kept until you leave Shelter Island or renounce it, and renouncing is permanent.
